question: How does the reference architecture enter the root hsdd-spec run: which files, with what authority?

options.label: Spec only
options.consequence: The root decomposes from the normative rules alone. Guide Appendix B (package layers) and Appendix C (what v1 ships) would be invisible, so v1 scope and the package split would rest on judgement.

options.label: Spec, Guide and Rationale, each with its authority
options.consequence: The root's Sources lists the Spec as the accepted normative source and the Guide and Rationale as informative. Downstream planners can read the Guide's Dart mappings and v1 tooling table; nothing informative can override a Spec rule.

options.label: All arch versions plus loop/
options.consequence: Superseded history would compete with v0.15.0 and the blindness rule forbids it.

chosen: Spec, Guide and Rationale, each with its authority
why: The owner's facts make the Spec accepted and frozen and the other two informative; hsdd-spec's Sources rule wants each input listed with its authority, and the Guide is the only place that says what v1 ships on Dart (Appendix C.2) and how the packages layer (Appendix B).

question: How is the run-stop condition 'two leading options change the tree's shape, the Specification is silent, no experiment settles it' read, given that the same policy lists v1 scope and decomposition shape under decide-and-record?

options.label: Literal
options.consequence: Every decomposition choice changes the tree's shape and the Spec says nothing about HSDD nodes, so the run would stop at the root on its first real choice; decide-and-record for decomposition shape would never apply.

options.label: Both defensible, no stated reason
options.consequence: The condition holds when the two leading options are both defensible, produce different nodes or contracts, and neither the Spec, the owner's facts, an experiment, nor a stated rule in the Guide, Rationale or HSDD gives one a reason to lead. Shape decisions with a stated reason are taken and recorded; the reason is cited as evidence.

chosen: Both defensible, no stated reason
why: Only this reading lets both halves of the policy apply. It keeps the stop for the case the policy is written for, a toss-up on shape that only the owner can break, and it is written into every subagent's prompt so the reading is visible and the same at every step. The signal that would have changed my mind: an owner statement that informative documents never break a shape tie.

question: The owner bans the em-dash and the phrase 'load-bearing' in prose; HSDD templates use an em-dash as a token (empty table cells, the OQ detail heading, the Collides-with reason). Which wins in HSDD artifacts?

options.label: Keep the HSDD template tokens
options.consequence: Artifacts match the templates character for character, and carry the character the owner bans.

options.label: Owner's ban, with parser-equivalent tokens
options.consequence: Empty cells and lists read `none`, OQ detail headings read `### {ID}: {title}`, a Collides-with reason is its own sentence. HSDD's parsers accept all three, so no tooling breaks.

chosen: Owner's ban, with parser-equivalent tokens
why: The owner's prose rules are standing instructions and HSDD's own tooling treats `none` as empty and a colon as the title separator, so honoring the ban costs nothing. Formatting only: no node, contract or interface changes.

question: The inputs include 'HSDD's own documentation under ~/git/hsdd/docs/'. Does that cover docs/superpowers/ and the Claude memory directory?

options.label: Everything under ~/git/hsdd/docs/
options.consequence: Subagents could read HSDD's development plans, which discuss field tests; one of them could describe the manual run of this planning.

options.label: users-guide and the methodology spec only; no memory, no docs/superpowers/
options.consequence: Subagents keep everything the methodology needs and lose HSDD's internal development notes, which no skill requires.

chosen: users-guide and the methodology spec only; no memory, no docs/superpowers/
why: The blindness rule forbids any document describing the manual run and forbids searching for one. HSDD's development notes and the session memory are the two places in reach that plausibly describe it, and the planning needs neither.

question: In what order do decomposition and contract authoring run?

options.label: Per level
options.consequence: Root spec, its ADRs, its contracts, then recurse; each mid-level decomposition reads concrete contract bodies for the edges it inherits. A root contract may need an amendment once its producer is decomposed.

options.label: Decompose everything first
options.consequence: All hsdd-spec runs first, then every contract once the whole tree is known; fewer amendments, but mid-level splits are cut against contract names and Spec prose rather than contract bodies.

chosen: Per level
why: HSDD's greenfield workflow is hsdd-spec (root), hsdd-contract, recurse; it keeps every decomposition cut against an interface that already exists. The cost, a draft contract amended after its producer splits, is cheap while contracts are draft. The signal that would have changed my mind: a root contract that the first mid-level decomposition has to split in two.

question: When does hsdd-reconcile run: once after every leaf-parent is planned, or after each phase plan?

options.label: Once at the end
options.consequence: Mirrors the parallel-worktree model; every plan is written against the same frozen snapshot, so a producer's amend and a consumer's assumption written blind to it can collide, which this run must stop on.

options.label: After each phase plan
options.consequence: Serial flow as hsdd-reconcile lists it ('a phase plan just finished in a serial flow'); each later plan reads contracts with earlier requests answered and amends folded in, so cross-node collisions cannot form from ignorance. Costs one reconcile step per leaf-parent plus a final sweep.

chosen: After each phase plan
why: The run is serial by rule, and with planning serial there is no reason to hide one node's settled contract from the next planner. Collisions that would come only from planning blind to an already-settled answer are artifacts of the parallel model, not design disagreements. A genuine disagreement still surfaces at the reconcile right after the plan that raises it. The signal that would have changed my mind: the owner wanting this run to exercise the parallel model's collision handling.

question: In what order are leaf-parents phase-planned?

options.label: Producer first (topological by contract edge)
options.consequence: A producer's plan, its amends and phase ids land before any consumer plans against the contract.

options.label: Tree order
options.consequence: Simpler to follow, but a consumer may plan against a contract whose producer has not settled its semantics yet.

chosen: Producer first (topological by contract edge)
why: With reconcile after each plan, producer-first order means each consumer reads the producer's settled contract. Ties break in tree order.

question: Which HSDD skills does this run use?

options.label: Planning skills only: hsdd-spec, hsdd-adr, hsdd-contract, hsdd-phase-plan, hsdd-reconcile
options.consequence: The run ends at reconcile as instructed; no phase context, milestone document, checkpoint or reading aid is produced.

options.label: Planning skills plus hsdd-milestone and hsdd-summary
options.consequence: The owner would also get a stakeholder milestone document and an HTML plan page, at the cost of steps outside 'through reconcile'.

chosen: Planning skills only: hsdd-spec, hsdd-adr, hsdd-contract, hsdd-phase-plan, hsdd-reconcile
why: The instruction is planning from scratch through reconcile, and the finish condition names no milestone or summary. hsdd-config is execution, hsdd-checkpoint and hsdd-intake need a running project, hsdd-adopt is brownfield.

question: Who runs experiments, and where do they land in the commit history?

options.label: The step subagent, inside its step
options.consequence: The experiment sits next to the decision it settles and lands in that step's artifact commit; the subagent spends part of its context on it.

options.label: Separate experiment subagents dispatched by the orchestrator
options.consequence: Cleaner step contexts, but every experiment breaks a step in two and the evidence lands in a commit apart from the decision.

chosen: The step subagent, inside its step
why: The decision and its evidence belong in one commit, and the subagent knows exactly which fact it needs. The orchestrator dispatches its own experiment subagent only when it needs a fact to answer a stop; that experiment is committed on its own as `experiment: <name>` and cited from the stop decision.

question: How are the skill's gates checked after each step?

options.label: Read-through only
options.consequence: The orchestrator reads every artifact against the skill's checklist; cheap to set up, and misses a stale registry or an unresolved id as easily as a person does.

options.label: Mechanical gate plus read-through
options.consequence: A dependency-free script checks write sets, the verbatim generator and a clean regeneration, id resolution, child files, Validation paths and the owner's prose bans; the orchestrator reads the rest against the subagent's self-check.

chosen: Mechanical gate plus read-through
why: The protocol's three named checks (clean regeneration, frozen governance changed only by its owner, every cited id resolves) are mechanical and run after every step; a script does them the same way every time. Judgement checks stay with the read-through.

question: What are the root node's id and name?

options.label: nidana
options.consequence: Shortest prefix for every dotted node id (nidana.runtime); the platform is already in the repository and package names.

options.label: nidana-bus
options.consequence: Closer to the product's full name; every node id gets four more characters.

options.label: nidana-bus-dart
options.consequence: Matches the repository name; repeats the platform in every node id.

chosen: nidana
why: Node ids are dotted paths from the root, so the root slug prefixes every id in the tree, every phase id and every OQ heading context. The repository name and the package names (nidana_dart_*) already carry the platform. No evidence beyond naming economy; the name is 'Nidana Bus for Dart and Flutter'.

question: hsdd-spec asks "who builds what?" before choosing an axis. The owner's facts answer it (Purbo alone with coding agents, one team, one repository). How does that answer shape the decomposition axis?

options.label: Capability slices along package boundaries
options.consequence: One owner holds the whole stack, so HSDD allows capability slices; slicing along published packages (the deploy targets) keeps each node one package and one contract surface.

options.label: Guide Appendix B layers one to one
options.consequence: One node per Guide B.2 package, including layers 2 and 3 that are not a real boundary on Dart and a test-utilities package that cannot be tested apart from the runtime.

options.label: Stack split between pure Dart and Flutter
options.consequence: Implies separate owners for the VM packages and the Flutter adapter, which the owner's facts deny; adds a Team field nobody uses.

chosen: Capability slices along package boundaries
why: The owner's facts state the team structure, so the axis question needed no stop. HSDD's axis rule (methodology spec §2.5) says vertical capability slices are correct when one owner holds the stack. Package boundaries are this tree's deploy targets and coincide with the Guide's library layers where a layer is a real dependency boundary on Dart; layers 2 and 3 are not, because RxDart is the only Dart engine (Guide §6.1).

question: Who are the package consumers?

options.label: App teams, their CI, pure Dart modules and the tree itself
options.consequence: Contracts and runtime stay usable without Flutter, so topology modules and VM tests depend on pure packages; the tooling has its own consumers (builds and CI).

options.label: Flutter app developers only
options.consequence: Simpler story, but nothing forces the contracts package to stay pure, and topology modules would be free to pull Flutter in.

chosen: App teams, their CI, pure Dart modules and the tree itself
why: The Specification makes topology definitions and transformers pure (Spec §5.3) and runs one bus per test (Spec §3.1), which only pays off if pure Dart code can depend on the contracts and runtime without Flutter. Build and CI consumers follow from the Spec's CI layers (Spec §3.11, §4.3, §4.5). GoTo Financial app teams as the first adopters is an assumption from the owner's context; if the first release is public pub.dev instead, only the publishing item changes.

question: Does navigation (Guide Appendix B layer 4, Guide §3) ship in v1?

options.label: Navigation in v1, executor in the Flutter adapter
options.consequence: Adds nidana.navigation and navigation-api@v1; the Flutter adapter ships FlutterNavigationExecutor as Spec Appendix A.8 says.

options.label: Navigation deferred
options.consequence: One node and one contract fewer; the Flutter adapter ships without the executor Spec Appendix A.8 attributes to it, and the deep-link bootstrap of Spec §3.13 has no reference implementation.

chosen: Navigation in v1, executor in the Flutter adapter
why: The two options produce different nodes, so this was checked against the tree-shape stop rule: the Specification gives inclusion a stated reason (Spec Appendix A.8 puts FlutterNavigationExecutor in nidana-runtime-flutter; Appendix A.6 defines the navigation vocabulary), and Guide B.4 draws the UI adapter on top of the navigation layer. Guide §3.7 calls navigation optional for apps, which D7 honors as opt-in by use. Signal that would have changed my mind: the owner saying the first adopting app keeps its own router-driven navigation.

question: Does persistence (Guide Appendix B layer 5) ship in v1?

options.label: Defer persistence
options.consequence: No persistence node; the hydration pattern of Spec §2.5 still works through events and reducers; persisted topics wait for a later release.

options.label: Include a persistence package
options.consequence: Adds a node whose design the Guide records as open (per-topic syntax, backend, migration, secure storage, hydration timing all open in Guide §10.5).

chosen: Defer persistence
why: Guide §10.5 lists every persistence question as open and says the package is in design; the Specification only constrains persistence that exists (Spec §9.2 item 3). Building it would mean deciding five open reference-architecture questions with no adopting app to test them. Signal that would bring it in: an owner-named v1 app that needs topic persistence.

question: Which Layer 7 tools ship in v1?

options.label: Guide's planned-v1 tools
options.consequence: Codegen, topic catalog, graph emission, the v1 checks and the build-time graph ship; v2 checks, runtime devtools and the perf suite wait.

options.label: No tooling in v1
options.consequence: A much smaller v1, but the Specification's CI layers (single-writer layer 2, CI name uniqueness, cycle and scope lints) would be missing although the Spec calls CI validation mandatory.

options.label: All of Appendix C, v2 included
options.consequence: Adds sequencer, orphan and purity analyses and runtime devtools the Guide itself schedules after v1.

chosen: Guide's planned-v1 tools
why: Spec §4.3 calls CI validation of topic names mandatory and Spec §3.11 enforces single-writer in two layers, one of them a CI scan; Guide Appendix C marks the codegen, the single-writer, scope and raw-string lints, the build-time visualizer and the TestBus recorder as planned v1. Following the Guide's own plan is the choice with a stated reason; the v2 items have one too (the Guide schedules them later).

question: Guide Appendix C.4 plans an OpenTelemetry exporter for v1. What ships?

options.label: SDK-neutral telemetry observer, SDK binding deferred
options.consequence: v1 ships the Guide §8.2 mapping as a BusObserver writing to ObserveContext.span; apps bind the span sink to any backend; no third-party SDK dependency.

options.label: Bind a concrete OpenTelemetry SDK in v1
options.consequence: A ready exporter, but tied to a pre-1.0 Dart SDK whose ecosystem is being renamed.

options.label: Defer telemetry entirely
options.consequence: Nothing to maintain, but the Guide's planned-v1 item is dropped although the mapping is cheap.

chosen: SDK-neutral telemetry observer, SDK binding deferred
why: pub.dev on 2026-10-17: package opentelemetry 0.18.11+1 is deprecated and re-exports opentelemetry_wk; dartastic_opentelemetry is at 0.12.0; opentelemetry_api last published 2022 for Dart 2. The observer seam (Spec §3.7) makes a binding an add-on, so the stable part, the mapping, ships now. Signal: the owner names a telemetry backend.

question: Spec §6.3 states a CI lint that warns when a service exposes a stream factory and also publishes; Guide Appendix C has no row for it. Is it in v1?

options.label: Defer it and report upstream
options.consequence: v1 checks match Appendix C; the gap between the Spec's sentence and the tooling plan is recorded for upstreaming.

options.label: Include it in the v1 checks
options.consequence: Closes the gap now, but adds an analysis the Guide never scoped and that needs cross-library data-flow knowledge.

chosen: Defer it and report upstream
why: Every other lint the Specification mentions has an Appendix C status; this one has none, so the Guide's plan gives no v1 reason. The Spec text reads as a description of tooling rather than a rule on the bus. Signal: a service in the example app that combines both and hides a data flow.

question: What is the root's child set, and what kind is each child?

options.label: Six children: model, runtime, navigation, flutter, tooling, integration
options.consequence: Pure core, runtime and tooling internal where they span mechanisms, navigation and Flutter as leaf-parents, one integration node.

options.label: One node per Guide B.2 package
options.consequence: Ten or more nodes, including an RxDart adapter split from a runtime that has one engine and a test-utilities package that cannot be tested apart from the runtime.

options.label: Contracts folded into the runtime
options.consequence: Five children; topology modules would depend on the RxDart runtime and the pure core would disappear as a unit.

chosen: Six children: model, runtime, navigation, flutter, tooling, integration
why: Guide Appendix B separates contracts, runtime, navigation, UI adapter and tooling as layers with their own dependents; Guide B.1 groups codegen, lint and devtools as one tooling layer, which is the stated reason for one internal tooling node rather than two root children. nidana.runtime and nidana.tooling each span several mechanisms (D4) and will not fit one phase plan; the leaf-parents each hold one scope one owner can keep in mind. Signal that would change the grouping: a second team taking the tooling.

question: Where do TestBus, the virtual scheduler and the envelope recorder live: in the runtime, or in a separate test-utilities node and package?

options.label: Inside nidana.runtime, as its testing.dart library
options.consequence: One node owns the bus and its test configuration; the runtime's own tests use the virtual scheduler; no package:test dependency in the runtime.

options.label: Separate nidana.testkit node and nidana_dart_test_utils package
options.consequence: Matches the package name Guide §6.5 and §10.1 use, but the runtime's tests need the virtual scheduler and the testkit needs the runtime, so neither can be tested alone.

chosen: Inside nidana.runtime, as its testing.dart library
why: The Specification defines TestBus as a bus constructed with a VirtualSchedulerProvider (Spec §3.6, Appendix A.7), and hsdd-spec says to merge two nodes that cannot be tested independently. The Guide's nidana-test-utils maps to the runtime's testing.dart (ADR-002 item 3). Signal: an app-facing matcher library on package:test, which would justify a separate package later.
evidence: .agents/skills/hsdd-spec/SKILL.md (merge when two nodes cannot be tested independently)

question: Does the contracts package hold only data types, or also the DSL interface, the recording builder and the IR analyses?

options.label: Contracts package holds DSL interface, recorder and pure analyses
options.consequence: Topology modules depend on a pure package; activation-time and CI checks run the same functions; tooling needs no runtime.

options.label: Data types only; DSL and analyses in the runtime
options.consequence: Matches a narrow reading of Guide B.1 layer 1, but topology modules and the tooling then depend on RxDart (Guide B.4 draws tooling on layer 3), and the same cycle and scope rules risk two implementations.

chosen: Contracts package holds DSL interface, recorder and pure analyses
why: Guide B.1 lists Topology in layer 1; Spec §6.5 makes the recorder and the IR pure; Spec §3.8 and §7.2 run the same checks at activation and in CI. The owner's functional-first preference (pure core, imperative shell) points the same way. Guide B.4's tooling-on-layer-3 edge is not followed: tooling never runs a bus.

question: Do the root's children need an integration node?

options.label: Add nidana.integration
options.consequence: A leaf-parent with hard edges to every producer replays fixtures live and runs end-to-end slices; scheduled last by the DAG.

options.label: No integration node
options.consequence: Each consumer's last phase composes what it consumes; nothing exercises the full stack, the example app and the CI checks together.

chosen: Add nidana.integration
why: hsdd-spec's integration-node rule: when an internal node's children exchange contracts, add a child leaf-parent named {node}.integration with hard edges to each producing sibling. The root's children exchange nine contracts.

question: Which contracts sit on the root's edges?

options.label: Nine contracts
options.consequence: topic-model, topology-dsl, topology-ir, bus-api, bus-testing, navigation-api, flutter-binding, topic-codegen, nidana-checks: one per distinct surface and validation kind.

options.label: One contract per package
options.consequence: Six coarser contracts; a package's value types, DSL and serialized IR would share one validation format although ADR-001 validates them differently.

options.label: Finer split
options.consequence: Eleven or more: separate contracts for the topics.yaml schema, the generated tree, the CLI and the analyzer diagnostics; more hsdd-contract steps for one consumer, the integration node.

chosen: Nine contracts
why: Each contract groups what one consumer set uses and one ADR-001 validation format can pin: value types (shared-model), the DSL and bus surfaces (api), the testing surface (api, separate consumers), the generated file layout (file), the CI-facing checks (cli). The tooling's input format and output tree share one file contract because the integration node and app builds consume them together. No external evidence; judgement on the consumer sets.

question: What do contract and shared-model edges mean between Dart packages, where a consumer cannot compile without the producer's declarations?

options.label: Start after the producer's first phase
options.consequence: Under fp-progression the first phase lands the contract's types and signatures; consumers start then, keeping the DAG's parallel lanes.

options.label: Type every Dart package dependency as hard
options.consequence: Honest about compilation, but every consumer waits for its producer's whole node and the lanes collapse into a chain.

chosen: Start after the producer's first phase
why: HSDD's contract edge means the consumer builds against the interface once it is stable (methodology spec §3.2); for Dart packages the interface is the producer's declarations, which the first phase lands under fp-progression. Hard edges stay where a consumer's tests need real behavior (runtime to Flutter, runtime testing surface to navigation).

question: What does executable validation (hsdd-contract's schema or fixtures) mean for this tree's contracts, most of which are Dart API surfaces? Proposed as ADR-001.

options.label: Compile, reject and conformance fixtures for Dart surfaces; JSON Schema for data
options.consequence: Positive compile fixtures pin signatures, negative ones pin type-level guarantees, package:test conformance libraries pin behavior and also validate implementations of interface contracts; data formats use JSON Schema; one replay tool runs them.

options.label: Language-neutral scenario fixtures
options.consequence: JSON scenarios run by an interpreter; answers Guide §10.1's cross-platform parity, but needs a scenario vocabulary and interpreter before any gate runs and cannot express type-level guarantees.

options.label: Public API snapshot diff
options.consequence: Pins signatures cheaply; pins no behavior and no type-level misuse.

chosen: Compile, reject and conformance fixtures for Dart surfaces; JSON Schema for data
why: The decision spans every contract and every producing gate, so it is cross-cutting and proposed as ADR-001. Many Specification guarantees are type-level (Spec §2.5, §3.7, §6.1 say a misuse does not compile) and the rest are behavioral (Spec §3). The experiment shows Dart files under the workspace root, outside every member, analyze and test against member packages, and that dart analyze --format=machine reports the code a reject fixture expects. Signal that would favor scenario fixtures: a second platform port starting within v1.

question: What package set and workspace layout does the tree use? Proposed as ADR-002.

options.label: Pub workspace at the repository root, Guide B.2 names, runtime layers in one package
options.consequence: One resolution and lockfile; members under packages/; contracts, runtime (layers 2 and 3), navigation, Flutter adapter, codegen, lint, a replay tool and the integration app; no rxdart-adapter, persistence, perf-suite, devtools or test-utilities package in v1.

options.label: Guide B.2 exactly
options.consequence: Separate nidana_dart_runtime_rxdart and nidana_dart_test_utils, navigation types in contracts: an engine abstraction with one implementation and a package that cannot be tested apart from the runtime.

options.label: Separate resolutions per package
options.consequence: Melos-style independence; contradicts the committed root lockfile and the no-melos note .gitignore already records.

chosen: Pub workspace at the repository root, Guide B.2 names, runtime layers in one package
why: .gitignore already records a pub workspace (root lockfile committed, non-member examples, no melos overrides). Experiments show a workspace resolving, analyzing and testing on the pinned SDK with pure Dart and Flutter members together, and contract fixtures resolving through the root (ADR-001 needs this). Guide B.2 names are kept for traceability where a package keeps its layer's role; the omissions in B.2 (no test-utilities or telemetry package although Guide §6.5, §10.1 and C.4 name them) are reported upstream. Signal that would split the runtime: a v1 requirement for a second engine such as plain dart:async streams.

question: Which static-analysis mechanism carries the v1 checks: custom_lint, which Spec §3.11 and Guide C.2 name, or the Dart 3.10 analysis server plugin API? Recorded in ADR-002 item 5.

options.label: Analysis server plugin, no custom_lint in the workspace
options.consequence: Rules run inside dart analyze and the IDE on the SDK's own analyzer (14.5.0); the workspace's single resolution stays current.

options.label: custom_lint as the Specification names it
options.consequence: Matches the text, but custom_lint 0.8.1 resolves only with analyzer 8.4.0 and drags the whole workspace's resolution (build, source_gen, analysis_server_plugin) back with it.

options.label: custom_lint in a non-member package
options.consequence: Keeps the workspace current, but the lint package then resolves apart from everything it checks and from the codegen it shares analyzer code with.

chosen: Analysis server plugin, no custom_lint in the workspace
why: Both mechanisms ran the same rule on the pinned SDK, so feasibility did not decide it; resolution did. One workspace has one resolution, and with custom_lint in it the analyzer is 8.4.0 instead of 14.5.0. The plugin API is the SDK's supported path since Dart 3.10. Reported upstream: Spec §3.11 and Guide C.2 name custom_lint.

question: How do Spec §3.6's SchedulerProvider and VirtualScheduler map onto Dart, where RxDart's time operators take no scheduler? Proposed as ADR-003.

options.label: Zone plus clock provider, own VirtualScheduler
options.consequence: The bus subscribes inside the provider's zone, so RxDart's own operators honor virtual time; production forks Zone.current; TestBus is synchronous; widget tests use tester.pump.

options.label: Reimplement time combinators against a scheduler interface
options.consequence: No zones, but the bus implements stream combinators, which Spec §2.3 says it does not, and duplicates RxDart.

options.label: Rely on fake_async in tests only
options.consequence: Least code, but fails whenever a bus is constructed or activated outside the fake zone, and SchedulerProvider gets no Dart meaning.

chosen: Zone plus clock provider, own VirtualScheduler
why: Experiments: fake_async controls RxDart timers only when the subscription was made inside its zone; DateTime.now() is not virtualized while clock.now() is; nested fake zones keep separate clocks; a bus-owned zone controls debounceTime, throttleTime and delay and captures the replay microtask and the Spec §3.4 deferral; under testWidgets a pass-through zone lets tester.pump drive the bus. RxDart 0.28.0 defines no scheduler type, although Guide §6.5 names an EventLoopScheduler for Dart: reported upstream. Rationale §3.2 makes full determinism under TestBus a stated property.

question: Guide §6.3's Dart example composes topology bodies with RxDart's Streams.combineLatest2 on read handles. Does the Dart DSL allow that?

options.label: Wrap every combinator in the model's DSL
options.consequence: The recorder captures every edge and the runtime threads envelopes; raw RxDart only through the Spec §3.5 escape hatch.

options.label: Allow raw RxDart on read handles as the Guide shows
options.consequence: Familiar Rx code, but the recording builder cannot capture it (Spec §6.5) and the bus cannot thread envelopes through it (Spec §3.5).

chosen: Wrap every combinator in the model's DSL
why: The Specification wins over the informative Guide: Spec §6.5 needs every combinator recorded and Spec §3.5 needs every stage to build the output envelope. Reported upstream: Guide §6.3 and the Combine row of Guide B.3 should show the wrapped form.

question: Where do the navigation types (NavIntent, RouteState, NavigationTopics) live: in the contracts package as Guide B.1 lists them, or in the navigation package?

options.label: Navigation package, with the Flutter adapter depending on it
options.consequence: The contracts package carries nothing navigation-specific; navigation is opt-in by use; the Flutter adapter ships the executor as Spec Appendix A.8 says.

options.label: Contracts package as Guide B.1 lists
options.consequence: Every app carries navigation types whether or not it navigates through the bus, contradicting Guide §3.7's opt-in package.

chosen: Navigation package, with the Flutter adapter depending on it
why: Guide §3.3 says the navigation topics are published by the navigation package and Guide §3.7 makes that package optional; Guide B.4 draws layer 6 on layer 4 and Spec Appendix A.8 puts FlutterNavigationExecutor in the Flutter adapter. Reported upstream: Guide B.1 lists the navigation ADTs in layer 1, inconsistent with §3.7.

question: What is dev mode on Dart, where do dev-mode diagnostics go, and is that an ADR?

options.label: BusConfig dev mode and typed diagnostics, carried by bus-api@v1
options.consequence: Defaults to assertions enabled; diagnostics are sealed values to a sink in BusConfig; one producer owns it and every node reads it through the contract; no ADR.

options.label: A cross-cutting ADR for diagnostics
options.consequence: Makes the mechanism a tree-wide decision file although only the runtime implements it.

options.label: Flutter's kDebugMode
options.consequence: Ties dev mode to Flutter, which the pure-Dart runtime must not import.

chosen: BusConfig dev mode and typed diagnostics, carried by bus-api@v1
why: The Specification requires dev-mode diagnostics (Spec §2.4, §3.4, §3.7, §3.13, §10.2) without defining dev mode. Assertions are on in debug and test runs and off in release builds on every Dart target; kDebugMode exists only in Flutter. HSDD keeps ADRs few and prefers a node-local decision when one producer owns the mechanism and others reach it through a contract.

question: Is the reactive engine and subject construction on Dart a cross-cutting ADR?

options.label: Node-local to nidana.runtime, timing surfaced in bus-api@v1
options.consequence: RxDart is fixed by the Spec and Guide; how subjects are built is the runtime's OQ-R1; consumers see only bus-api@v1 guarantees.

options.label: A cross-cutting ADR
options.consequence: Records engine and subject construction tree-wide, although no node other than the runtime touches a subject.

chosen: Node-local to nidana.runtime, timing surfaced in bus-api@v1
why: Spec §2.1 and §3.3 and Guide §6.1 already fix RxDart for Dart. The experiment found facts the runtime's design must handle (asynchronous first delivery of sync behavior and replay subjects, StateError on same-subject reentrant add, depth-first delivery across subjects); they are recorded at the root (D9) and handed to OQ-R1. Reported upstream: Spec §3.3 says no machinery beyond sync: true is needed for RxDart.

question: Which ordering policy does conventions.md declare?

options.label: fp-progression
options.consequence: Types, pure functions, effects, composition as four bands; the first phase lands every produced contract's declarations, unblocking contract and shared-model edges.

options.label: interfaces-first
options.consequence: HSDD's default; interfaces first and composition last, with pure and effectful middle phases in any order.

chosen: fp-progression
why: The owner's standing preference is functional-first, pure core and imperative shell; the model node is pure end to end and the runtime separates pure decisions (ownership, lifecycle state) from effects. Both policies put the contract skeleton first, so D10's edge semantics hold either way. Signal that would favor interfaces-first: phase plans finding effect-free bands too thin to earn a cycle under the sizing floor.

question: Which OQ prefixes do the node specs use?

options.label: One letter per child, one more letter per grandchild
options.consequence: M, R, N, F, T, I for the six children; a child of an internal node appends a letter (RA, RB) declared when it is created.

options.label: Numbered prefixes
options.consequence: Stable but unreadable at a glance (OQ-C1 for which child?).

chosen: One letter per child, one more letter per grandchild
why: Readable ids that grep to their owner, and a rule that lets later hsdd-spec runs mint prefixes without colliding. Judgement only; no evidence.

question: How do the template's OpenSpec-specific sections of conventions.md adapt to the superpowers method without dropping the template's structure?

options.label: Keep every section, rewrite the OpenSpec ones for superpowers
options.consequence: Same section order; Layout swaps openspec/ for docs/superpowers/plans/; 'OpenSpec init' becomes 'Execution setup (superpowers)'; sizing counts plan tasks; the execution protocol swaps config.yaml and capability naming for per-phase context and plan files; each rewritten section says what it replaces.

options.label: Delete the OpenSpec sections
options.consequence: Shorter file, but later skills and readers lose the template's anchors.

options.label: Keep them verbatim and add a superpowers note
options.consequence: Template-identical, but the file would instruct an openspec init the owner forbids.

chosen: Keep every section, rewrite the OpenSpec ones for superpowers
why: The owner fixes superpowers and forbids installing OpenSpec. hsdd-config's superpowers derivative starts at writing-plans, saves plans under docs/superpowers/plans/ and reads the task count from the phase's size estimate, so the sizing line keeps HSDD's wording and redefines the unit. The standalone-spec-repo profile section stays and says it is unused.

question: Child-owned open questions whose answers shape a root-level contract (OQ-M1 to OQ-M3, OQ-R1 to OQ-R3, OQ-N1, OQ-N2, OQ-F1) come up before the owning node's own step runs. Resolve them at the root now, or mint them in the owning child as OPEN?

options.label: Mint in the owning child as OPEN, waiting on the contract step
options.consequence: The producer's contract author decides the interface; the row names that step; the owner node's next step or hsdd-reconcile's sweep marks it resolved.

options.label: Resolve them at the root now
options.consequence: No open rows, but the root would design contract interfaces that hsdd-contract owns, ahead of the contract author reading the full Interface.

chosen: Mint in the owning child as OPEN, waiting on the contract step
why: The decision policy allows child-owned questions minted OPEN for the child's own step; these are owned by the producing node, and the run plan authors root contracts (stage 4) before the owning node's decomposition or phase plan, so the contract step is where each gets decided. Conventions now say so in the OQ section.

question: What kind is topology-ir@v1, whose content is Dart types and analysis functions plus a JSON form?

options.label: api with a serialized form
options.consequence: Surface, reject and conformance fixtures pin the Dart types and analyses; a JSON Schema and edge cases pin topology-graph.json; ADR-001 item 2 allows the combination.

options.label: schema
options.consequence: Pins the JSON form only; the analyses the runtime and the tooling call stay unpinned.

chosen: api with a serialized form
why: Spec §6.5 defines the IR as Dart values with toGraph and renderers, and Guide C.3 emits topology-graph.json for CI. Both consumer sets need pinning: the runtime and tooling call the analyses; external CI tools read the JSON.

question: Materialize ADR-001 as accepted, or as proposed with the Decision left as a TODO?

options.label: accepted
options.consequence: binding at once; hsdd-config injects its Decision and Consequences into every phase context that touches a contract, and the nine contract steps author fixtures in its format

options.label: proposed with TODO
options.consequence: hsdd-adr's rule for a decision the human has not stated; every contract step would lack a binding fixture format

chosen: accepted
why: The owner's decision policy accepts every proposed ADR, and the decision content is not invented: it is the root decomposition's proposal plus the sharpenings recorded below, each with evidence from docs/auto-run/experiments/contract-fixtures/.

question: Filename slug and title of ADR-001.

options.label: 001-executable-contract-validation, root title kept
options.consequence: the slug names the topic, which covers all five kinds; the title matches the root's heading, OQ8 and every citation

options.label: 001-dart-api-contract-validation
options.consequence: mirrors the title but understates the schema, file and cli items

options.label: retitle to Executable contract validation
options.consequence: more accurate, but the root heading and OQ8 detail would read differently from the file

chosen: 001-executable-contract-validation, root title kept
why: hsdd-adr asks for a 2 to 4 word topic slug; the topic is executable validation of every contract kind, while the title keeps the id and wording the root already uses. No evidence beyond naming consistency.

question: Fixtures live under hsdd/ at the workspace root, belong to the root package, and reject fixtures hold deliberate errors. How are they kept out of workspace-wide analysis, and which analysis options apply to them?

options.label: root excludes hsdd/**, fixture-local options with no lints and strict modes
options.consequence: workspace-wide fvm dart analyze never sees a fixture; the replay tool analyzes explicit paths under hsdd/contract/fixture/analysis_options.yaml, which drops the root lint set and turns on strict-casts, strict-inference, strict-raw-types; ADR-002's root options gain one exclude

options.label: root lints apply, root dev-depends on members
options.consequence: depend_on_referenced_packages silenced by dependencies, but a workspace-wide analyze still fails on every reject fixture and on bindings whose producer is absent, so an exclude is needed anyway; fixture verdicts then depend on whatever lint set the root adopts

options.label: replay copies fixtures into a temporary package
options.consequence: isolation, but the copy sits outside the workspace and loses its package resolution

chosen: root excludes hsdd/**, fixture-local options with no lints and strict modes
why: The experiment shows the exclude hides fixtures from a workspace-wide analyze while an explicit path is still analyzed, and that a nested analysis_options.yaml replaces the root lint set (without it depend_on_referenced_packages fires on every import). Strict modes make a surface fixture fail on raw types and inference failures, which catches signatures that leak dynamic into consumer code; a lint set would make fixture verdicts depend on style rules unrelated to the contract.

question: How does a reject fixture name its expected diagnostic, and when does it pass?

options.label: line-anchored marker, exact match at every severity
options.consequence: a `// expect-diagnostic: {code}` comment on its own line expects {code} (lowercase, as --format=json reports it) on the next line, like `// ignore:`; the file passes when reported (line, code) pairs at every severity equal the marked pairs; catches wrong lines, extra diagnostics and wrong codes, and pins warning-severity guarantees such as @visibleForTesting

options.label: file-level header, errors only (root proposal)
options.consequence: simpler to write, but passes a marker on the wrong line and a misuse that fails for another reason in the same file, and cannot pin a warning-severity guarantee

options.label: Dart SDK static-error test markers with columns
options.consequence: column-precise, but verbose and tied to SDK test tooling that is not a pub package

chosen: line-anchored marker, exact match at every severity
why: The prototype in the experiment passes the good set and fails the three broken cases (wrong line, extra diagnostics, a plausible but wrong code authored without running the analyzer), all of which a file-level, errors-only match lets through in part. JSON output gives the lowercase code and 1-based line directly. If fixtures turned out to need column precision (two misuses on one line), the SDK marker format would win.

question: What shape does a behavior fixture take so one suite validates implementations that need different test runners (VM and widget tree)?

options.label: cases as values plus per-implementation bindings
options.consequence: a conformance library declares a harness interface (factories plus settle()) and exports List<ConformanceCase<H>>, a record ({String name, Future<void> Function(H) body}) shared through package:nidana_contract_check/fixture.dart; it asserts with package:matcher/expect.dart and imports no test runner; each binding registers the cases with test or testWidgets

options.label: suite registers its own tests (root proposal wording)
options.consequence: a function taking factories that calls test() itself; cannot obtain a WidgetTester, so a Flutter implementation needs a second suite that drifts

options.label: one suite per runner
options.consequence: no shared abstraction, two copies of every guarantee

chosen: cases as values plus per-implementation bindings
why: The experiment binds one conformance library under test on the VM and under testWidgets with pumpAndSettle, from the same file. Cases as values keep the suite pure data and the binding a thin shell, which is the owner's functional-first preference. The shared record alias lives in the replay tool's library so every suite uses one shape; a per-suite inline typedef would also work structurally and was the close alternative.

question: Where do bindings live, who writes them, how are they named, and how are they bound before the producing package exists?

options.label: in the fixture directory of the contract that declares the implementation, written by hsdd-contract
options.consequence: behavior/{implementation}_test.dart next to the suite, or importing another contract's suite by relative path (bus-api@v1 binds topology-dsl@v1's live builder; flutter-binding@v1 binds navigation-api@v1's executor); every contract step writes only its own directory; the producer's gate exercises the bound suite; bindings are forward references until the producer's first phase lands; the Validation section lists each binding

options.label: in each implementing package's test/, written by its phases
options.consequence: bindings compile from day one of the package, but a phase could bind a subset of cases and HSDD keeps fixtures out of phase hands

options.label: in the suite's own directory for every implementation
options.consequence: one place per suite, but the navigation-api@v1 step would write a binding against flutter-binding@v1's surface before that contract exists

chosen: in the fixture directory of the contract that declares the implementation, written by hsdd-contract
why: hsdd-contract: 'Authoring writes the artifact' and 'A phase never writes them'. Placing a binding with the contract that declares the implementation means the producer of that contract replays it with no cross-node selection, and the producer-first order of the contract steps (execution plan S06..S14) already writes each suite before its foreign bindings. A consumer's stand-in, which no contract declares, is the one binding a phase writes, in its own test/ directory by relative import (Q15).

question: What does the replay do with a binding whose implementing package does not exist yet?

options.label: fail, reported as PENDING
options.consequence: a mis-scheduled gate cannot pass; the message tells an absent producer apart from a failing case; nidana.integration's --all run fails until every producer exists

options.label: skip with a warning
options.consequence: early gates stay green, but a renamed or missing package passes a gate silently

options.label: author bindings only once the package exists
options.consequence: no pending state, but every contract needs a second hsdd-contract pass after its producer's first phase

chosen: fail, reported as PENDING
why: Under the binding-location rule, a binding is only pending when a replay runs before its own producer's first phase, which no gate should do; failing keeps that visible. The workspace package configuration identifies the absent package before running (Q14). Had bindings been placed in the suite's directory for foreign implementations, skipping would have been needed and the decision would flip.

question: How does the replay choose the test runner for a binding, and from which directory does it run?

options.label: by import, from the workspace root, pinned SDK
options.consequence: a binding importing package:flutter_test runs under flutter test --no-pub, any other under dart test, both from the root; flutter is derived from the dart running the tool, so both use the fvm pin

options.label: a runner header in each binding
options.consequence: explicit, but a header can disagree with the imports

options.label: run each binding from its implementing package's directory
options.consequence: matches Flutter habits, but the tool must map bindings to packages and the root already works

chosen: by import, from the workspace root, pinned SDK
why: flutter test --no-pub runs a binding under hsdd/ from the pure-Dart workspace root, and dart test cannot load it, so the runner must be chosen per binding; the import cannot lie. The tool's Platform.resolvedExecutable is the fvm-pinned SDK's dart inside the Flutter SDK, so the matching flutter is derivable.

question: How is the replay tool invoked from a gate?

options.label: one CLI: fvm dart run nidana_contract_check {slug}... [--set] [--guarantee] or --all
options.consequence: one command per gate line; sets structure, surface, reject, behavior, schema, file, cli; structure always runs first and needs no implementation; one line per fixture, non-zero exit on any failure

options.label: a script per set
options.consequence: simpler tool, longer and drift-prone gate lines

options.label: a package:test meta-suite
options.consequence: familiar output, but analysis and recorded invocations fit awkwardly in test cases

chosen: one CLI: fvm dart run nidana_contract_check {slug}... [--set] [--guarantee] or --all
why: dart run {member} works from the workspace root without the root depending on the member, so the gate line is short and needs no path. A --binding selector was considered and dropped: with bindings placed by declaring contract, every binding in a slug's directory belongs to that slug's producer.

question: Which fixture sets does an intermediate producing phase's gate run, when later phases deliver the remaining behavior?

options.label: type-level sets in full, behavior restricted cumulatively, unrestricted at the last producing phase
options.consequence: phase 1 (the skeleton under fp-progression) already passes surface and reject; each later gate names the guarantee ids delivered so far; the last phase producing the contract runs everything

options.label: every set in full at every phase
options.consequence: gates fail until the last phase, so they stop meaning anything

options.label: behavior only at the last phase
options.consequence: simple, but behavior regressions surface late

chosen: type-level sets in full, behavior restricted cumulatively, unrestricted at the last producing phase
why: fp-progression makes phase 1 land every declaration of every contract the node produces (conventions), so surface and reject can pass from the first gate, while behavior lands phase by phase. A test-name prefix filter selects cases under both runners (Q9, Q11). This assumes one leaf-parent lands all of a contract's declarations; see notes for nidana.runtime's decomposition.

question: What must an api or shared-model fixture set minimally contain to count as the executable validation artifact at hsdd-reconcile's draft to stable flip, given that reconcile itself only checks that the path exists?

options.label: guarantee ids with full coverage
options.consequence: every guarantee bullet begins `- **G{n}**`, stable per slug; each is covered by a reject fixture (`// covers: G{n}`) or a behavior case named 'G{n} ...', or listed as `not executable` with the node gate that checks it; surface/ uses the whole Interface; bindings listed in Validation exist; the structure set checks this once the tool exists, reading does until then

options.label: existence only (HSDD default)
options.consequence: one placeholder file satisfies stable; the root's success criterion that every Spec §3 guarantee is covered becomes uncheckable

options.label: a coverage matrix in the Validation section
options.consequence: readable in one place, but a second source of truth beside the fixture headers that drifts

chosen: guarantee ids with full coverage
why: The root's success criteria require every Bus Runtime Contract guarantee to be covered by a contract fixture or a node test a gate runs; ids make that mechanically checkable, and the coverage relation lives in the fixtures themselves. hsdd-config injects the Guarantees section verbatim, so phase contexts carry the ids that gates cite in --guarantee. No runtime evidence; this is a format choice the decision policy assigns to this step.

question: Which schema dialect and validator, and how does the producer's gate check its real output against the schema?

options.label: draft 2020-12 via package:json_schema; producer side as behavior cases
options.consequence: the schema set checks valid/ validates and invalid/ does not, with no producer; the round trip of every valid/ file and the schema check of real output are cases in the contract's conformance library, through expectMatchesSchema in package:nidana_contract_check/fixture.dart; json_schema joins the workspace resolution

options.label: draft-07
options.consequence: wider tool support, no unevaluatedProperties, so closed objects composed from $defs cannot be stated

options.label: an emitter command named in Validation
options.consequence: the tool validates a command's stdout; one more protocol to keep beside the behavior bindings

chosen: draft 2020-12 via package:json_schema; producer side as behavior cases
why: json_schema 5.2.2 validates $defs, prefixItems, items: false and unevaluatedProperties under draft 2020-12 and resolves alongside Flutter and test in one workspace. Putting the producer-side check in the conformance library reuses the binding mechanism instead of adding a second one.

question: What exact protocol do file and cli replays follow?

options.label: generator command with placeholders; invocation directories with path normalization
options.consequence: file: Validation names a command with {input} and {output}, run into an empty directory, generated Dart formatted, compared byte for byte with expected/; cli: invocation/{case}/ with args, optional files/ as working directory, exit_code, optional stdout and stderr compared after {files} and {root} substitution; a plugin case enables nidana_dart_lint in files/analysis_options.yaml by relative path; topic-codegen must expose a command entry outside build_runner

options.label: bindings for file and cli too
options.consequence: one mechanism, but every recorded invocation becomes Dart test code and the recorded outputs stop being plain files a reviewer reads

chosen: generator command with placeholders; invocation directories with path normalization
why: Plain recorded files are what HSDD's per-kind table asks for (a sample tree, recorded invocations). The experiment shows an input tree under hsdd/ enabling an analysis server plugin by relative path, also when the plugin is a workspace member, and that JSON and machine output carry absolute paths, hence the normalization.

question: What slug does the ADR file take?

options.label: 002-package-workspace-layout
options.consequence: Three-word kebab slug naming both halves of the topic, within hsdd-adr's 2 to 4 words.

options.label: 002-package-and-workspace-layout
options.consequence: Mirrors the title word for word; five words, over hsdd-adr's slug length.

options.label: 002-pub-workspace
options.consequence: Shorter, but drops the package set, which is half of the decision.

chosen: 002-package-workspace-layout
why: hsdd-adr asks for a 2 to 4 word kebab slug of the decision topic; this one keeps both the package set and the workspace. Naming only, no evidence needed.

question: Does the package set and naming of the root's proposal hold on the pinned SDK (eight members under packages/, Guide B.2 names where a package keeps its layer's role, layers 2 and 3 folded into nidana_dart_runtime, no rxdart adapter, persistence, perf-suite, devtools or test-utilities package)?

options.label: Keep the proposal's package set and names
options.consequence: Eight members, traceable to Guide B.2; the experiment builds and tests a stand-in of exactly this set in one workspace with a Flutter member.

options.label: Guide B.2 exactly
options.consequence: Adds nidana_dart_runtime_rxdart and a test-utilities package: an engine abstraction with one implementation and a package that cannot be tested apart from the runtime.

options.label: Add a separate scan or checks package
options.consequence: A ninth package with a clearer name for the aggregate checks; the scan would then share the topology catalog scan with the codegen across a package boundary.

chosen: Keep the proposal's package set and names
why: The stand-in workspace (wl_* for nidana_*) resolves, analyzes, tests and runs build_runner with this exact set on Flutter 3.47.7 / Dart 3.13.5. The fold of layers 2 and 3 and the absence of a test-utilities package rest on root D3 and D4 (RxDart is the only engine, TestBus cannot be tested apart from the runtime). The reasons root S02 marked for upstreaming (Guide B.2 omits the test-utilities and telemetry packages) still hold. Signal that would split the runtime: a v1 requirement for a second engine.

question: Does the analysis server plugin stay the static-analysis mechanism once the real single resolution is known (the proposal's rationale said that without custom_lint 'the SDK's analyzer 14.5.0 resolves')?

options.label: Analysis server plugin, no custom_lint
options.consequence: Rules run under dart analyze and the IDE; the workspace resolves analyzer 13.3.0, the best a resolution holding Flutter and test can reach.

options.label: custom_lint as Spec §3.11 and Guide C.2 name
options.consequence: Matches the text, but custom_lint 0.8.1 requires analyzer ^8.0.0 and would hold the whole workspace at 8.4.0.

options.label: custom_lint in a package outside the workspace
options.consequence: Keeps the workspace current, but the lint package resolves apart from what it checks and from the codegen.

chosen: Analysis server plugin, no custom_lint
why: The proposal's claim of analyzer 14.5.0 was measured without Flutter. With Flutter and test in the same resolution, flutter_test's test_api 0.7.12 pin holds test at 1.31.1, whose test_core caps analyzer below 14, so the workspace gets 13.3.0 (Q1, Q2). The comparison still favors the plugin: 13.3.0 against custom_lint's 8.4.0, which pub.dev's custom_lint 0.8.1 (analyzer ^8.0.0) forces. Corrected in the ADR's Context and in OQ9's detail. Marked for upstreaming: Spec §3.11 and Guide C.2 name custom_lint.

question: What does the root analysis_options.yaml contain beyond the proposal's excludes?

options.label: lints/recommended plus strict-casts, strict-inference, strict-raw-types
options.consequence: Every member inherits one lint set and the strict modes ADR-001's surface fixtures use; a member surface that leaks dynamic fails its own analyze before it fails a surface replay. The root gains lints as its only dev dependency.

options.label: Excludes only
options.consequence: No shared lint set; implementation_imports and depend_on_referenced_packages go unchecked, and a dynamic leak shows only at the surface replay.

options.label: flutter_lints for every member
options.consequence: Adds Flutter-specific rules to pure Dart packages and a Flutter package to the root's dev dependencies.

chosen: lints/recommended plus strict-casts, strict-inference, strict-raw-types
why: The experiment shows members without an options file inherit the root's lint set and strict modes, and the recommended set's implementation_imports enforces the proposal's 'public libraries only' rule (Q11). ADR-001 analyzes surface fixtures under the same strict modes, so code and fixtures agree. lints 6.1.0 resolves beside Flutter. Signal that would change it: Flutter-specific rules wanted in nidana_dart_runtime_flutter, which a member options file that includes the root's can add.

question: ADR-001 follow-up: does the root's exclude list add hsdd/** beside ref/** and docs/**?

options.label: Exclude ref/**, docs/** and hsdd/**
options.consequence: Workspace-wide analysis never reports a fixture's deliberate errors; the replay tool analyzes fixtures by explicit path.

options.label: Rely on the nested fixture options file only
options.consequence: Reject fixtures' deliberate errors would fail every workspace-wide analyze.

chosen: Exclude ref/**, docs/** and hsdd/**
why: ADR-001 Decision item 2 and its Consequences require it, and its experiment shows the exclude hides fixtures from a workspace-wide analyze while explicit paths still analyze. This experiment adds that the excludes also hide a nested package under docs/ whose options name a nonexistent plugin (Q11), and that ADR-001's nested fixture options keep the root-enabled plugin off fixtures (Q11d). ref/ holds no Dart file today; its exclude is free.

question: Does the root workspace: list name members explicitly or by glob?

options.label: Explicit member list
options.consequence: Every member is added deliberately by the phase that creates it, matching 'one owning node per package'; the root pubspec.yaml changes with each new member.

options.label: Glob packages/*
options.consequence: The root pubspec never changes, but any directory under packages/ joins the resolution without an owner.

chosen: Explicit member list
why: Globs work on the pinned SDK (Q4; Dart 3.11+ per the pub workspaces page), so the choice is not forced. An explicit list makes membership a reviewed change and keeps a stray directory out of the single resolution. Cost: phases that create members edit the same file, which phase planning must serialize with Collides with. Signal that would change it: many parallel member-creating phases colliding on the root pubspec.

question: How do members declare dependencies on each other: hosted version constraints or path dependencies?

options.label: Hosted version constraints
options.consequence: The workspace resolves them to the local member and the member stays publishable unchanged; outside the workspace they resolve against pub.dev, so consumers before publication need overrides.

options.label: Path dependencies
options.consequence: Resolve inside and outside the workspace, but every publishable member then fails dart analyze with invalid_dependency and fails pub publish.

chosen: Hosted version constraints
why: A hosted constraint resolves to the local member, and a version mismatch fails resolution loudly (Q3); a member with hosted sibling constraints passes publish validation except for metadata (Q16); a path dependency in a publishable package is an analyzer warning that fails the root analyze and a publish error (Q11, Q16). The pub workspaces page shows the same form.

question: How are third-party version constraints written across members that share one resolution?

options.label: Caret on the locked version, same constraint in every member
options.consequence: The lower bound is a version the lockfile actually tested, and members never disagree on a package's range.

options.label: Each member chooses its own constraints
options.consequence: Less coordination, but lower bounds below the locked version go untested and ranges drift between members.

options.label: any everywhere
options.consequence: No bookkeeping, but published packages carry no meaningful bounds and pub warns at publish.

chosen: Caret on the locked version, same constraint in every member
why: One lockfile tests one version of each package, so only a lower bound equal to that version is tested; pub publish validation also asks for real constraints (Q16 shows the warning for unconstrained dependencies). Judgement beyond that; no experiment compares the alternatives. Signal that would change it: a published release that must support adopters on older dependency versions, which would need a pub downgrade gate.

question: Where do example/ folders go: non-member packages with uncommitted lockfiles (the proposal), nested workspace members, or plain folders inside their member with no pubspec?

options.label: No pubspec: part of the member
options.consequence: An example analyzes with its member and uses its dependencies; no extra resolution; the runnable example app stays nidana_integration.

options.label: Non-member example packages
options.consequence: The root pub get also resolves each member's example/ outside the workspace, where an unpublished sibling cannot be found, so it fails with exit 69.

options.label: Nested workspace members
options.consequence: Works, but each example adds a package to the single resolution and its pubspec ships in the parent's archive.

chosen: No pubspec: part of the member
why: The proposal's option breaks the root pub get on the pinned SDK (Q6a): pub get resolves example/ folders by default, outside the workspace. Nested members work (Q6b) but buy nothing nidana_integration does not already provide. A pubspec-free example analyzes and runs as part of its member (Q6c). This changes the proposal's item 6; .gitignore's comment about non-member examples becomes a case that never occurs.

question: ADR-001 follow-up on the plugin mechanism: where is nidana_dart_lint enabled so that dart analyze runs its rules?

options.label: Workspace root options, added by the phase that creates the plugin
options.consequence: The rules run over every member, the tree's own packages included; a plugin that does not build fails every root analyze, so every gate depends on the plugin's health.

options.label: nidana_integration's own options
options.consequence: Would scope the rules to the example app, but the analyzer rejects plugins in a member's options (plugins_in_inner_options).

options.label: Recorded invocations only
options.consequence: A broken plugin never fails a member's gate, but no member, the example app included, is ever checked by dart analyze.

options.label: nidana_integration outside the workspace
options.consequence: Its own options may then enable the plugin, but it needs its own resolution and lockfile, path dependencies plus overrides for every package, and gates that resolve twice.

chosen: Workspace root options, added by the phase that creates the plugin
why: The analyzer accepts a plugin only in the options at the root of a pub workspace (Q11, and dart.dev's analyzer-plugins page says 'at the root of your package or workspace'). Enabled there, it reports in every member (Q11b); a broken plugin fails analyze with exit 3 (Q11c), which is loud rather than silent. ADR-001's nested fixture options keep it off surface and reject fixtures (Q11d), and recorded invocations still enable it by relative path (contract-fixtures Q19, workspace-layout Q13, Q15). Running the rules over the tree's own packages also checks that they obey Spec §3.1 and §4.4 themselves.

question: The analysis server resolves a plugin in its own synthetic package outside the workspace, where a hosted constraint on an unpublished sibling fails. Where do the workspace scan and the checks that need nidana_dart_contracts' analyses (root D4) run?

options.label: Command entry of nidana_dart_codegen; nidana_dart_lint depends on no nidana package
options.consequence: The plugin keeps per-library rules only and loads anywhere; the aggregate checks run the model's analyses from a package that already depends on contracts and owns the catalog scan and graph emission.

options.label: nidana_dart_lint with a path dependency on contracts and publish_to: none
options.consequence: Keeps Guide C.2's grouping and loads as a plugin (Q13), but the package is unpublishable until edited, and per-library plugin rules have no use for aggregate analyses.

options.label: A separate scan package
options.consequence: Clearer naming, a ninth package, and the scan shares the catalog scan with the codegen across a package boundary.

chosen: Command entry of nidana_dart_codegen; nidana_dart_lint depends on no nidana package
why: Runtime facts: a plugin with a hosted constraint on an unpublished sibling fails to load (Q12); a path dependency loads (Q13) but is an analyzer warning and a publish error in a publishable package (Q11, Q16). Stated reasons for the codegen as host: Spec §3.11 says the single-writer scan feeds the topology graph generator so that they 'share infrastructure', Guide C.3 lists the codegen's topology-graph.json as the CI lint manifest for cycle detection, and root D4 requires the CI checks to call the same analyses activation calls. Plugin rules see one library at a time (OQ-T2's premise), so they need none of those aggregate analyses. Partially resolves OQ-T2; the scan's inputs stay with nidana.tooling. Changes the proposal's 'lint holds the workspace scan'. Signal that would change it: a plugin rule that must run the model's analyses inside the IDE.

question: How does nidana_dart_lint constrain analyzer and analysis_server_plugin, given that the plugin runs under the synthetic package's resolution while its tests run under the workspace's?

options.label: Exact pins to the lockfile's versions
options.consequence: Both resolutions agree (13.3.0 and 0.3.18); the pins move with the SDK pin, and a published plugin works only with servers that accept 0.3.18.

options.label: Open or caret constraints
options.consequence: The synthetic package resolves analyzer 14.5.0 and analysis_server_plugin 0.3.24 while tests ran on 13.3.0 and 0.3.18: the shipped plugin runs code no test ran.

chosen: Exact pins to the lockfile's versions
why: Q14 shows the skew with open constraints; Q15 shows exact pins make the synthetic package resolve the workspace's versions and the plugin load on the pinned SDK, whose server asks for analysis_server_plugin ^0.3.8. analysis_server_plugin itself pins analyzer exactly per release (0.3.24 pins 14.5.0), so the two versions move as a pair anyway. analyzer_testing 0.3.2 resolves beside 13.3.0 for rule tests (Q17).

question: ADR-001 follow-up: does the codegen's command entry that runs outside build_runner (the file replay of topic-codegen@v1) belong in this ADR or in the codegen contract?

options.label: Package shape here, command interface in the contract
options.consequence: This ADR fixes that nidana_dart_codegen has bin/ command entries over the same pure generator functions as its builders; topic-codegen@v1 and nidana-checks@v1 fix executable names, arguments and outputs.

options.label: Leave all of it to topic-codegen@v1
options.consequence: The contract author decides whether a command exists at all, after the package layout is fixed; nidana-checks@v1's scan command would have no fixed host.

chosen: Package shape here, command interface in the contract
why: The ADR says why and the contract says what (hsdd-adr). Whether a package has executables, and that builders and commands share one pure generator, is package shape across two contracts and the integration node; the arguments are an interface. Q8 shows a command entry calling the builder's pure function writes byte-identical output from the workspace root, and Q9 that dart run {package}:{executable} works there.

question: ADR-001 follow-up: what is nidana_contract_check's full dependency set, given it joins the single resolution?

options.label: args, json_schema, matcher, package_config, path; test as dev
options.consequence: Covers ADR-001's CLI, schema validation, the fixture.dart exports asserting with matcher, and PENDING detection from the package configuration.

options.label: json_schema only
options.consequence: What ADR-001 names, but fixture.dart's matcher-based assertions and the package_config read would add undeclared imports that depend_on_referenced_packages reports.

chosen: args, json_schema, matcher, package_config, path; test as dev
why: ADR-001 items 4 and 9: fixture.dart exports ConformanceCase and expectMatchesSchema (json_schema plus matcher), the tool parses --set and --guarantee (args) and tells a PENDING binding from the workspace's package configuration (package_config). All resolve in the full stand-in workspace with Flutter (Q1); a stand-in fixture.dart compiles against them. Matcher is pinned by flutter_test to 0.12.20.

question: May a published member list test or flutter_test under dependencies (for example the Flutter adapter's widget-test helpers taking a WidgetTester)?

options.label: Neither test nor flutter_test in a published member's dependencies; matcher allowed
options.consequence: The runtime's testing.dart and the adapter's helpers serve VM and widget tests alike; helpers cannot take a WidgetTester, so a test calls tester.pump itself.

options.label: Allow flutter_test in nidana_dart_runtime_flutter
options.consequence: Helpers can extend WidgetTester; every app's main dependency graph then carries flutter_test and its exact pins.

options.label: A separate Flutter test package
options.consequence: WidgetTester helpers without touching the adapter's dependencies, at the cost of a ninth package.

chosen: Neither test nor flutter_test in a published member's dependencies; matcher allowed
why: Extends the proposal's 'testing.dart has no dependency on package:test' to the Flutter adapter for symmetry; matcher stays allowed because ADR-001's conformance libraries show it works under both test and testWidgets. Judgement: no experiment shows a helper that needs WidgetTester. Signal that would change it: the flutter-binding@v1 author finds a helper that cannot be written without WidgetTester, which would supersede this item. Recorded in nidana.flutter.md's widget-test library line.

question: What strictness does the workspace-wide analyze hold?

options.label: Clean under fvm dart analyze --fatal-infos at the root
options.consequence: Lint infos and the plugin's rules, which report at INFO severity, fail analyze; every member is held to the lint set.

options.label: Default dart analyze (warnings and errors fail)
options.consequence: Lint infos and every plugin rule pass silently, so the v1 checks never fail a gate.

chosen: Clean under fvm dart analyze --fatal-infos at the root
why: The plugin's warning rules report at INFO severity (Q11b, Q11d, Q13), so without --fatal-infos the v1 checks cannot fail anything. ADR-001's surface fixtures already pass under --fatal-infos.

question: Which SDK constraint do the members declare?

options.label: ^3.13.0, the Dart of the .fvmrc pin
options.consequence: The bound is what the tree tests; adopters need Dart 3.13 (Flutter 3.47) or later.

options.label: A lower bound such as ^3.11.0
options.consequence: Wider adoption on older Flutter releases, but no gate tests that bound.

chosen: ^3.13.0, the Dart of the .fvmrc pin
why: Nothing in the tree tests a lower SDK, and publishing is out of v1 (root D1), so the bound matters only at publication, where widening it is non-breaking. Signal that would change it: an owner-named adopting app pinned to an older Flutter.

question: How are member versions managed before v1?

options.label: Lockstep from 0.1.0; unpublished members carry no version
options.consequence: One version for every published member; a bump touches every version and inter-member constraint in one change.

options.label: Independent semver per package
options.consequence: Finer releases, but inter-member constraints drift and a one-owner tree gains nothing from independent cadences.

chosen: Lockstep from 0.1.0; unpublished members carry no version
why: Kept from the proposal. With hosted sibling constraints, a version that no longer satisfies a sibling's constraint fails resolution (Q3), so lockstep bumps keep the workspace resolving. 0.1.0 is the conventional first pre-release on pub. Signal that would change it: a package with a separate consumer base that needs its own release cadence.

question: Do published members carry pub metadata files in v1, although publishing is an owner action?

options.label: README, CHANGELOG and a copy of the repository LICENSE in each published member
options.consequence: pub publish --dry-run reports no error, so publication needs only the owner's repository field and credentials.

options.label: Leave metadata to the publishing action
options.consequence: Less to write now; every package then fails publish validation until edited.

chosen: README, CHANGELOG and a copy of the repository LICENSE in each published member
why: Q16 shows a missing LICENSE is the only publish error of a member laid out this way; README and CHANGELOG are the remaining recommendations. The repository already carries an Apache-2.0 LICENSE, so no licensing choice is made here. The repository field and publication stay with the owner.

question: Does the ADR fix library naming inside members, which contract fixtures import by package URI?

options.label: Main library lib/{name}.dart; other public libraries named by their contract; the rest under lib/src/
options.consequence: Fixtures can name main-library URIs now; contracts own the names of extra public libraries such as testing.dart.

options.label: Leave library names to each contract
options.consequence: No rule to break, but nine contract steps choose names without a convention.

chosen: Main library lib/{name}.dart; other public libraries named by their contract; the rest under lib/src/
why: ADR-001 fixtures import package:{name}/{library}.dart and ban src/ imports, so every contract needs public library URIs. The main-library convention is pub's default and matches the publish validator's naming check (Q16 flags lib/main.dart only because the plugin requires that name). The plugin's lib/main.dart is the one stated exception, required by the analysis server's synthetic entry point.

question: Which ids does affects name: the seven nodes of the proposal only, or also the nine contracts?

options.label: Seven nodes and all nine contracts
options.consequence: Every contract file carries Governed by ADR-002, so contract authors see the package names, library rules and the codegen and lint hosts the Interfaces depend on.

options.label: Seven nodes only
options.consequence: Phases still receive the ADR through their nodes, but contract steps would not be pointed at the package and library names their fixtures import.

chosen: Seven nodes and all nine contracts
why: Every contract's fixtures import a package URI this ADR fixes, bus-testing@v1 and flutter-binding@v1 are shaped by the test-framework rule, and topic-codegen@v1 and nidana-checks@v1 by the command and plugin hosts. ADR-001 set the same precedent. Contract ids are forward references until their files exist.

question: OQ-T2 asks where the single-writer workspace scan runs. With item 8 fixing its host, does the row stay OPEN or become PARTIAL?

options.label: PARTIAL, residual: what the scan reads
options.consequence: The row points at ADR-002 for the host and leaves the scan's inputs to nidana.tooling's decomposition.

options.label: Leave OPEN
options.consequence: The tooling decomposition would reopen a host the package layout already fixed.

chosen: PARTIAL, residual: what the scan reads
why: The conventions define PARTIAL with the residual under Waits on, and hsdd-adr asks that an ADR resolving an OQ updates its owning spec's row. The three options OQ-T2 lists (analyzer scan, catalog IR plus AST scan, both with IDE surfacing) all remain open and all fit a codegen command.

question: What slug does the ADR file take?

options.label: 003-time-source-virtual-scheduler
options.consequence: Four words naming both halves of the decision, the production time source and the test scheduler; within hsdd-adr's 2 to 4 words.

options.label: 003-time-source-scheduler
options.consequence: Three words, but drops 'virtual', which is what TestBus readers search for.

options.label: 003-virtual-scheduler
