question: Does topic-model@v1 carry a JSON Schema?

options.label: no schema
options.consequence: the Interface's Dart declarations are the schema (ADR-001 item 4); the JSON encodings of TopicRef, Scope and MessageSource go to topology-ir@v1's schema

options.label: a schema for TopicRef and MessageSource
options.consequence: a second home for an encoding the IR's schema must also state

chosen: no schema
why: ADR-001 item 4: api and shared-model contracts carry no schema unless they have a serialized form; this contract has none of its own.

question: S06 suggests an optional hsdd-adr touch that adds topic-model@v1 to ADR-003's affects, so the contract header could carry Governed by ADR-003. Run it?

options.label: Run the hsdd-adr touch
options.consequence: One more step; hsdd-config would inject ADR-003's Decision into every phase that consumes topic-model@v1, which is nearly every phase of the tree.

options.label: Leave affects as it is
options.consequence: ADR-003 keeps governing nidana.model, the producer, so the producer's phases still receive it; the contract carries the obligation as its own guarantee G25 and cites ADR-003 item 8 in prose.

chosen: Leave affects as it is
why: The obligation ADR-003 puts on this contract (no clock, no scheduling, timestamps and ids as arguments) binds the producer, which ADR-003 already governs, and the contract states it as G25. Injecting ADR-003 into every consumer's phase context would add a long Decision to phases it does not constrain. The signal that would change this: a consumer-side obligation from ADR-003 on topic-model values.

question: Which signature makes writing a handle of the wrong value type to a topic a compile error (Spec §4.2), given that Dart generics are covariant and inference solves a type argument two arguments constrain to their least upper bound?

options.label: write<T>(Topic<T>, TopicStream<T>)
options.consequence: the Guide B.3 shape, but an unrelated or a wider stream compiles as write<Object>; Spec §4.2's guarantee does not hold

options.label: write<T, S extends T>(Topic<T>, TopicStream<S>)
options.consequence: keeps the b.write(topic, stream) shape; an unrelated or wider stream is one could_not_infer error, a subtype stream into a supertype topic compiles

options.label: stream.writeTo(topic)
options.consequence: rejects unrelated types, but rejects the sound subtype case and admits the unsound wider case

options.label: b.write(topic).from(stream)
options.consequence: sound and permissive, but a new call shape and a dangling write target when .from is forgotten

options.label: invariant handle via a function-type typedef
options.consequence: sound but rejects sound subtype writes, reports two diagnostics per misuse and exposes an obscure typedef

chosen: write<T, S extends T>(Topic<T>, TopicStream<S>)
why: The probe shows it is the only form that keeps the Spec and Guide call shape while rejecting both unsound cases with a single diagnostic and accepting the sound subtype write. Explicit type arguments that widen T still bypass it; the live publish then fails at run time, which no form avoids.

question: How do the recording and the live implementations of the DSL relate: two implementations of a builder interface, or one recording builder whose plan a live implementation interprets?

options.label: two builder implementations
options.consequence: matches the 'live builder' wording of ADR-001 item 4; declare() runs twice per activation (record for checks, then wire live); handles must be an implementable interface, so a handle from one builder passed to the other fails only at run time and apps can implement handles

options.label: one recording builder, plan interpreted live
options.consequence: declare() runs once; the IR and the live wiring come from one plan by construction; handles, builder and stages are closed types; the runtime implements a StageVisitor over a public plan library; bus-api@v1 declares an activation path, no live builder type

chosen: one recording builder, plan interpreted live
why: The Specification says the bus interprets the recorded declaration (Spec §2.2 'inert data', §2.5 'the bus interprets this metadata on activation', §6.5 'the bus interprets the same IR for live activation, ensuring the graph and the running system are structurally identical', A.1, A.4). Dart has no higher-kinded types, so a builder interface with two implementations cannot type its handles per implementation. The owner's functional-first practice (an immutable ADT and its interpreters, pure core and imperative shell) points the same way. ADR-001 item 4's binding rule still holds: the live binding lives with bus-api@v1, which declares the live implementation. The signal that would have favored two builders: a live behavior the plan cannot express, which no Spec §6.3 combinator needs.

question: OQ-M2: How does live activation obtain the transformers a pure-data IR names?

options.label: executable beside FunctionRef in the IR
options.consequence: matches the Spec wording, but the IR holds functions excluded from equality and JSON, so it is no longer pure data

options.label: record, then run declare() again live
options.consequence: the IR stays pure, but every activation runs declare twice and relies on its determinism for the checked IR to equal what is wired

options.label: one plan, IR projected from it
options.consequence: declare runs once into a TopologyPlan holding the functions; activation checks plan.definition and interprets the same plan; the IR stays pure data

chosen: one plan, IR projected from it
why: It keeps both properties the two original options trade against each other: a pure-data IR and a single declare run, so the checked definition and the live wiring cannot disagree. Recorded as Refinement 3 and G18. nidana.model's phase planning marks the OQ-M2 row.

question: OQ-M1, DSL side: does every combinator take an explicit transformer name?

options.label: explicit name parameter
options.consequence: stable names under --obfuscate and for closures, at the cost of a parameter on every combinator

options.label: no name parameter; the plan keeps the function
options.consequence: the plan holds each function identical to what was passed, and topology-ir@v1 derives FunctionRef from it; closures and obfuscated builds need its fallback

chosen: no name parameter; the plan keeps the function
why: Spec §6.2 asks for named standalone functions, whose tear-off toString() carries the name in JIT and AOT without obfuscation, and the build-time catalog runs on the VM. TopologyBuilder and TopicStream are final, so adding an optional name parameter later is compatible. The signal that would favor the parameter: an owner need for transformer names in an obfuscated release build's runtime graph. The derivation rule and its fallback remain for topology-ir@v1.

question: What is the Dart surface of a topology and its combinators: builder functions only, or methods on the handle, and how closed are the types?

options.label: builder functions only
options.consequence: the Kotlin form combine(a, b, f), map(s, f); no chaining

options.label: Spec and Guide split
options.consequence: read, write, reduceInto, combineN, combineAll and merge on the builder; single-input combinators and withLatestFrom on the handle (Spec §6.1 .map, Guide B.3 a.withLatestFrom, a.switchMap); Topology an @immutable abstract base class with a @nonVirtual buildDefinition(); TopologyBuilder final; TopicStream sealed

chosen: Spec and Guide split
why: It follows Spec §6.1 and Guide B.3's Dart rows, wrapped per root D6. Topology is a base class so no type can implement it with a definition unrelated to its declaration (Spec §6.5); the cost is that a subclass is declared final class, where Guide §6.3's Dart example writes class. Arities: combine2 to combine4 with combineAll, withLatestFrom to withLatestFrom3, which covers the Guide §3.4 resolver; nesting or combineAll covers more.

question: Which combinators does the v1 DSL provide beyond the Spec §6.3 table, and how are the Spec's error operators (retryWhen, catchError, onErrorResumeNext) realized on Dart?

options.label: Spec §6.3 table plus the three named error operators
options.consequence: a pipeline-level retryWhen must re-subscribe a shared upstream, which is ill-defined for event topics and for shared stages; onErrorResumeNext duplicates catchError for the Guide §4 use

options.label: curated: table, merge, timeout, catchError, retry on switchMap
options.consequence: merge lets a reducer fold several event topics; timeout is a Spec §3.6 time operator; catchError turns a shell failure into a value; retry belongs to the switchMap inner stream, where the effect is, as a pure policy timed on the provider clock

chosen: curated: table, merge, timeout, catchError, retry on switchMap
why: Errors in a DSL pipeline originate in shell streams (Spec §6.3 'effectful stream sources'), so retrying means calling the stream factory again, which is what the switchMap retry does; ADR-003 item 4 anticipates a timed retry. onErrorResumeNext's documented use, fallback state (Guide §4), is catchError. merge is not in Spec §6.3's table but is needed for reducers over several event sources and has trivial lineage; recorded for upstreaming with the error-operator mapping.

question: Does the DSL provide a switch that selects among topic pipelines (Spec §6.1 and §7.1 'switchMap ... to select between pipelines'), beside switchMap over a shell stream factory?

options.label: switchAmong(candidates, select)
options.consequence: expresses the Spec's wording directly, but a selected candidate either is re-subscribed cold, which breaks stage sharing (G27) and runs shared effects twice, or stays shared and hot, which loses a state candidate's current value on selection or replays a past event

options.label: no selecting switch
options.consequence: selection between state-like pipelines is a combine over the configuration topic; between event pipelines, a withLatestFrom gate per pipeline joined by merge; both pipelines stay subscribed

chosen: no selecting switch
why: The stand-in live implementation showed the conflict between a switch among shared stages and the replay semantics of reads; existing combinators express both selection cases exactly. This reverses the inclusion I had first drafted. The signal that would bring it back: a pipeline whose inactive branch is expensive to keep subscribed. Spec §6.1, §7.1 and Guide §10.4 describe the selection as switchMap; recorded for upstreaming.

question: What does an unhandled error in a live pipeline do on Dart, where a stream error does not end the stream?

options.label: the sink it reaches ends
options.consequence: matches Spec §10.2's model (an error terminates the pipeline, the bus logs it in dev mode and does not restart it) and Rx engines on other platforms; the topology's other sinks go on

options.label: the error is reported and the pipeline goes on
options.consequence: more resilient, but a topology would behave differently on Dart than the Specification describes

chosen: the sink it reaches ends
why: Spec §10.2 items 2 and 4 describe termination, and nidana.runtime already owns 'dev-mode logging of terminated pipelines'. The error is never rethrown; reporting goes to the D8 sink. The signal that would favor going on: an owner preference for Dart-native resilience over parity with the Specification.

question: Is a stage evaluated once for all its consumers, or once per consumer, in a live activation?

options.label: shared within an activation
options.consequence: a function runs once per input value and a switchMap's shell factory once per outer value; fan-out order is defined; the runtime must connect reads after wiring every consumer

options.label: one chain per consumer
options.consequence: the Rx default for cold streams; a stage used twice runs its function twice and its shell effect twice

chosen: shared within an activation
why: A switchMap into a service's stream factory consumed by two sinks would otherwise call the service twice, an effect the topology author cannot see; Spec §3.3's fan-out guarantee presupposes one emission feeding several outputs. Connection after wiring makes activation-time replays reach every consumer, whichever first-delivery timing OQ-R1 picks.

question: Which sinks does Spec §3.3's fan-out order cover?

options.label: every sink one emission reaches
options.consequence: the order would depend on how many stages lie between the emission and each sink, which an implementation cannot keep in declaration order without global scheduling

options.label: sinks that take the same handle
options.consequence: the Spec's 'single transformer produces emissions to multiple output topics'; deliverable by subscribing sinks in declaration order

chosen: sinks that take the same handle
why: Spec §3.3 states the guarantee for one transformer's emissions; a sink behind another stage receives a different transformer's output.

question: What does recording do with a stage that reaches no sink?

options.label: record it
options.consequence: Spec §6.5's 'captures all calls'; the definition then shows a read that nothing live performs

options.label: prune it
options.consequence: the definition matches the live wiring, but a forgotten write passes silently

options.label: reject the declaration
options.consequence: planOf throws StateError; a forgotten write fails at activation and in the catalog; conditional wiring on a build-time flag must keep its read inside the condition

chosen: reject the declaration
why: A handle that feeds nothing is almost always a forgotten write, and rejecting it keeps the definition and the live wiring identical. The signal that would favor pruning: topology modules that routinely build handles under build-time flags.

question: Where does the plan library live?

options.label: in the main library
options.consequence: every topology module sees stages, visitors and planOf

options.label: a second public library, topology_plan.dart
options.consequence: a topology module, importing the main library alone, cannot name a stage or obtain a plan (G2); the runtime, tooling and tests import both

chosen: a second public library, topology_plan.dart
why: Only interpreters, the catalog and tests read plans; ADR-002 item 3 lets a contract name a further public library of its package.

question: Is ADR-003 item 3's live switchMap property (cancel the previous inner without waiting, listen to the next at once) a guarantee of topology-dsl@v1 or of bus-api@v1?

options.label: topology-dsl@v1
options.consequence: the property sits with the combinator it constrains, is observable through the live harness without bus types, and is bound by the live binding bus-api@v1 writes

options.label: bus-api@v1
options.consequence: bus-api@v1 would restate switchMap's semantics in its own suite

chosen: topology-dsl@v1
why: It is a property of a combinator this contract defines; the live binding of this suite runs it anyway (G22). The case checks synchronously after a virtual advance with a cancel future that never completes, so both RxDart 0.28's wait and its root-zone hop fail it (run.sh T11).

question: What do the time-dependent combinators emit, given that ADR-003 item 4 makes them RxDart 0.28's operators or Stream.timeout?

options.label: RxDart and SDK semantics as they are
options.consequence: sample and buffer periods count from the first value; throttle is leading only; timeout raises one error per silence; buffer emits empty lists after its first window

options.label: those semantics, with buffer never emitting an empty batch
options.consequence: the runtime drops RxDart's empty windows; every batch has a value whose lineage it carries

chosen: those semantics, with buffer never emitting an empty batch
why: Read from the sources: RxDart 0.28 BufferStreamTransformer passes ignoreEmptyWindows: false and sample and buffer use WindowStrategy.firstEventOnly; throttleTime defaults to leading: true, trailing: false; the SDK's Stream.timeout arms a one-shot timer re-armed only by an input event and captures Zone.current when timeout() is called. An empty batch has no lineage and is noise for batching analytics (Spec §6.3).

question: What lineage does a value carry that catchError produces from an error, and that a read delivers for a state topic's declared initial value?

options.label: always Lineage.root()
options.consequence: simple, but a recovered failure no longer points at the value that caused it

options.label: the most recent value through the stage
options.consequence: trivial to implement, but a switchMap failure would point at the previous query

options.label: the lineage the raising stage would have passed
options.consequence: a recovered value's cause is the input that failed; errors without such a value (timeout, raw operator) recover as a new flow; the runtime carries lineage with each error internally and unwraps it for recover and for raw operators

chosen: the lineage the raising stage would have passed
why: Causation exists to answer 'why did this happen' (Spec §2.4); for a failure the answer is the value whose processing failed. A state topic's initial value was caused by no message, so a read delivers it with Lineage.root(), which topic-model@v1 leaves unstated.

question: Which stages mediate an intra-topology self-reference (Spec §3.8) for topology-ir@v1's analysis?

options.label: scan and reduceInto only
options.consequence: the Spec's explicit example; time-shifting chains that cannot loop in zero time are rejected

options.label: scan, reduceInto, and debounce, delay, sample and buffer with a positive duration
options.consequence: follows the Spec's second clause, 'a stateful operator chain that cannot loop back to the read in zero time'; the IR must carry those durations

chosen: scan, reduceInto, and debounce, delay, sample and buffer with a positive duration
why: Those stages emit only on a timer, so a write fed back to their read cannot re-enter them within one instant; throttle emits its leading value synchronously and does not qualify. The signal that would narrow it: topology-ir@v1 choosing not to carry durations, in which case it treats them as not mediating.

question: What does the raw-engine escape hatch hand the author: envelopes or pipeline values?

options.label: Stream<MessageEnvelope<T>>
options.consequence: the Spec §3.5 wording, but the author would mint ids and timestamps the contracts package cannot provide, and intermediate envelopes are invisible by topic-model@v1's per-published-message rule

options.label: Stream<PipelineValue<T>> with a fresh-correlation source
options.consequence: the author applies topic-model@v1's Lineage functions; errors arrive as the objects stages raised

chosen: Stream<PipelineValue<T>> with a fresh-correlation source
why: topic-model@v1 computes lineage per published message, and nidana_dart_contracts mints no id and reads no clock (topic-model@v1 G25); a Lineage.combine in a raw operator needs a correlation source, which the live implementation provides. Recorded for upstreaming: Spec §3.5's escape hatch on Dart applies lineage functions rather than constructing envelopes.

question: OQ-R3 (nidana.runtime), DSL side: what does a read deliver under the per-read dedup opt-out, and does this contract fix where dedup sits?

options.label: read semantics only
options.consequence: this contract fixes what each read delivers (G19, Dedup.none delivering an equal publish); where suppression sits and what observers see stay with bus-api@v1

options.label: also fix the placement
options.consequence: this contract would decide observer and recorder visibility, which are bus-api@v1's guarantees

chosen: read semantics only
why: What a read delivers is DSL semantics; what an observer sees is the publish path's. Either placement OQ-R3 lists satisfies G19.

question: How are the conformance cases organized so that both the recording and the live implementation can be bound, without this contract naming bus types?

options.label: one library, one harness
options.consequence: the harness would need both recording and live capabilities, and the recording binding could not supply the live ones

options.label: two libraries, two harnesses
options.consequence: recording_conformance.dart (RecordingHarness, settle only) bound here; live_conformance.dart (LiveTopologyHarness with LiveRun: start, publish, watch, deliveries, current, advance, activate, deactivate, settle) bound by bus-api@v1's step

chosen: two libraries, two harnesses
why: Recording and live guarantees need different capabilities; ADR-001 item 4 allows several conformance libraries per contract, and its binding rule puts the live binding with bus-api@v1. The live harness is stated in topic-model and topology-dsl types and Duration only; a stand-in binding on a virtual scheduler passed all 43 live cases.

question: What is the recording binding named?

options.label: nidana_dart_contracts_test.dart
options.consequence: S06's name, after the package

options.label: topology_builder_test.dart
options.consequence: named after the implementation it binds, as ADR-001 item 4 asks; S06's implementation was the package's declarations themselves

chosen: topology_builder_test.dart
why: The implementation here is the recording builder, TopologyBuilder; ADR-001 item 4 names a binding after its implementation. No evidence beyond that rule.

question: Does topology-dsl@v1's Governed by list ADR-003, whose affects omits this contract while its items 3 and 4 constrain it?

options.label: [ADR-001, ADR-002]
options.consequence: agrees with every ADR's affects; G22 and G23 cite ADR-003 items in their text

options.label: [ADR-001, ADR-002, ADR-003]
options.consequence: names the ADR that constrains the switchMap and time guarantees, but disagrees with ADR-003's affects until an hsdd-adr touch adds the contract

why: As S06 did, Governed by mirrors the ADRs' affects; the fix is an ADR-003 touch through hsdd-adr, after which this line gains ADR-003. The signal that would change it: an orchestrator convention that Governed by lists every ADR the text cites.

question: What do produced_by, consumers and external_consumers name?

options.label: node ids, provisional
options.consequence: S06's rule; phase planning confirms phase ids through hsdd-reconcile

options.label: guessed first phase ids
options.consequence: phase plans do not exist yet; every id would be a guess

chosen: node ids, provisional
why: Same reason as S06: no phase plan exists. consumers lists nidana.runtime (which also implements the live side), navigation, flutter, tooling and integration, as the root contract matrix does; external consumers are app topology modules and app topology tests.

question: Does this contract declare a typed topology identifier?

options.label: declare TopologyRef
options.consequence: the Spec §4.6 example and Guide C.5's v2 lint have a type to name; modules keep their references private

options.label: leave typed ids to modules
options.consequence: each module invents its own wrapper

chosen: declare TopologyRef
why: Spec §4.6 names TopologyRef in its Dart example and Guide C.5 lints exported TopologyRef values; a one-field value costs nothing.

question: S07 asks for two governance touches: add topology-dsl@v1 to ADR-003's affects (ADR-003 items 3 and 4 constrain its live guarantees G22 and G23), with ADR-001 item 4's wording 'live topology builder' aligned to the plan-interpretation path; and correct the root's OQ5 detail, which says server rewiring is 'covered by topology-dsl@v1's switchMap'. When do these run?

options.label: One touch step each, now
options.consequence: Each fix lands immediately, at the cost of interleaving small hsdd-adr and hsdd-spec steps between contract steps, and of re-touching the same ADRs again if later contracts raise similar links.

options.label: Batch after the last root contract
options.consequence: One hsdd-adr step after S14 fixes every ADR affects and Governed-by link and any ADR wording the nine contracts exposed; one root hsdd-spec touch fixes root prose. Until then the gate keeps reporting the links as warnings, and contract steps read the contracts, which already state the binding facts.

chosen: Batch after the last root contract
why: Neither touch blocks a contract step: S07's contract states the guarantees ADR-003 constrains, and S09 is told where the live binding goes. The next seven contracts are likely to expose more links of the same kind (bus-api@v1 and bus-testing@v1 against ADR-003, flutter-binding@v1 against ADR-001's binding rule), and one pass over them costs less than several. The signal that would change this: a contract step that misreads an ADR because of a missing link.

question: How does TransformEdge represent a pipeline of several stages, a write and a reduceInto, when Spec §6.5 sketches an edge with topic references at both ends?

options.label: Spec sketch literally
options.consequence: one edge per sink whose inputs are the upstream topics; a chain read, map, filter, write cannot be described, so the self-reference check of Spec §3.8 cannot inspect paths and the graph has no internal nodes

options.label: Edges over topic or stage inputs, sinks as edges
options.consequence: an edge's inputs are TopicInput (a read, with its dedup argument) or StageInput (an earlier edge); a write and a reduceInto are sink edges with an output topic; one list carries the whole DAG and keeps the Spec's field names; a write has no CombinatorKind, so combinator is nullable for writes; deviates from the Spec sketch

options.label: Separate sinks list
options.consequence: a sixth definition field for sinks; reduceInto, which has a CombinatorKind and is a sink, straddles both lists; analyses walk two structures

options.label: Sealed edge class per kind
options.consequence: exact typing per combinator, but eighteen or more classes that every consumer switches over and every new combinator breaks

chosen: Edges over topic or stage inputs, sinks as edges
why: Spec §3.8 and Guide C.1 define the intra-topology check as inspection of TopologyDefinition.transforms for paths from read to write through stateful operators, so the IR must carry the stage DAG; the Spec sketch cannot. One list with the Spec's field names is the smallest deviation, and CombinatorKind stays at the eighteen values topology-dsl@v1 fixed (a write is the edge with no combinator, validated by three named constructors). The edge also records the read's dedup argument and switchMap's retry reference, because Spec §3.9 makes any observable difference between two activations of one id an error and bus-api@v1 will most likely compare definitions. Signal that would have changed it: consumers that need typed per-kind access often, which would favor a sealed per-kind family.

question: OQ-M1: How does the recorder name a transformer (FunctionRef) in Dart?

options.label: Derive from toString, VM pattern only
options.consequence: FunctionRef.of reads the name between "from Function '" and the next quote; named on the VM and in AOT, stable obfuscated names under --obfuscate, anonymous on dart2js and dart2wasm and for closures; no DSL change; a static method loses its class

options.label: Derive with a dart2js fallback
options.consequence: names on web builds too, but dart2js names inline closures main_closure and minified builds minified:xx, so closures would get false names

options.label: Explicit name on each combinator
options.consequence: exact names everywhere at the cost of a name argument on every call; a change topology-dsl@v1 lists as not in v1

options.label: Optional explicit name, then derivation, then a positional placeholder
options.consequence: flexible, but placeholders make definition equality depend on stage position and need a topology-dsl@v1 amendment

options.label: Leave naming to the static catalog
options.consequence: definitions from buildDefinition() carry no names, so the runtime graph and the static graph differ, against Spec §6.5's single IR

chosen: Derive from toString, VM pattern only
why: The experiment shows JIT and AOT render the names of top-level functions, static methods (without class) and method tear-offs, obfuscated AOT renders stable obfuscated names, dart2js renders compiler-internal names even for inline closures, and dart2wasm renders none. The catalog and the CI checks, which are where names are read, run on the VM; Spec §6.2 makes transformers named standalone functions; topology-dsl@v1's Versioning already answers OQ-M1 by derivation here. Equality is by name, so recording one declaration twice gives equal definitions even with inline closures (topology-dsl@v1 G9). Signal that would have changed it: a v1 consumer needing names in web builds, or static methods of one name in different classes colliding in practice; either brings an optional explicit name as a compatible topology-dsl@v1 addition.

question: Does the IR carry the durations of debounce, delay, sample and buffer, or does the self-reference analysis treat them as not mediating?

options.label: Carry durations
options.consequence: isStateBearing holds for those four with a positive duration, as topology-dsl@v1's Self-reference column states; graph labels and definition equality see durations

options.label: Treat them as not mediating
options.consequence: a smaller IR, but a debounce feedback loop that Spec §3.8 allows (a stateful chain that cannot loop back in zero time) would be rejected, and topology-dsl@v1's table would need an amendment

chosen: Carry durations
why: topology-dsl@v1 already marks the four stages as mediating when the duration is positive, and Spec §3.8 accepts a stateful chain that cannot loop back in zero time; carrying the duration decides the rule from the IR alone and costs one optional field. A zero duration does not mediate, which the findings sample exercises.

question: Which public library carries the IR, the graphs, the renderers, the JSON codec and the analyses?

options.label: All in the main library
options.consequence: one import for every consumer; every topology module's namespace also carries renderer, codec and analysis names such as JsonRenderer

options.label: Value types in the main library, the rest in topology_ir.dart
options.consequence: buildDefinition(), which modules call, returns types the main library has; the runtime, tooling and tests import a second library; module namespaces stay small

options.label: Everything in topology_ir.dart
options.consequence: impossible without changing topology-dsl@v1, whose surface fixture uses TopologyDefinition through the main library alone

chosen: Value types in the main library, the rest in topology_ir.dart
why: topology-dsl@v1's surface fixture reads TopologyDefinition from the main library, so the value types must be there; nothing in a topology module needs a renderer or an analysis. ADR-002 item 3 lets the declaring contract name a second public library. The case is close: the signal that would have changed it is app topology tests that routinely render graphs, which would favor one library.

question: Does a definition take reads and writes as arguments, or derive them from its edges?

options.label: Derive them
options.consequence: the constructor takes id, scope and edges; an inconsistent definition cannot exist; the JSON form still lists reads and writes for CI tools, and the decoder rejects a document whose lists disagree with its edges

options.label: Take them as arguments
options.consequence: matches the Spec sketch's five constructor fields and eases hand-built test definitions, but a definition can then contradict its own edges

chosen: Derive them
why: A pure core should make the inconsistent value unrepresentable; tests build definitions by recording topologies, which yields consistent edges anyway. The redundant lists stay in the JSON form, where CI tools that need only reads and writes per topology (cycles, orphans) read them without walking edges.
evidence: Guide C.3 (topology-graph.json for cycle detection and orphan analysis)

question: How does a shell publisher's claim and its scope enter the scope-compatibility and single-writer analyses without this contract naming a bus type?

options.label: ShellClaim values inside TopologyGraph
options.consequence: a claim is (MessageSource source, Scope scope defaulting to application, Set<TopicRef> state topics); the graph holds topologies and claims; bus.toGraph() and the catalog build the same type; claims appear as source nodes in renderings, as Spec §3.11 describes

options.label: A separate ownership argument to each analysis
options.consequence: graphs stay topology-only, but every analysis grows a parameter, renderings cannot show shell writers, and the static and live views diverge

options.label: Model claims as pseudo-topologies
options.consequence: no new type, but a claim has no edges or reads, its source is not a topology id, and cycle and self-reference analyses would have to skip them

chosen: ShellClaim values inside TopologyGraph
why: Spec §3.11 has publisher claims appear as source nodes in the topology graph and Spec §7.2 gives each claimant a scope, application when unbound; one value with those three parts carries exactly that. Writers are identified by MessageSource, the identity their publishes already carry (TopologySource for a topology), so findings name the current owner as Spec §3.11 requires. A claim rejects topology and unknown sources, an empty set and non-state topics, since only state topics are claimed (Spec §2.4).

question: What does a graph do with two definitions of one topologyId, and with two equal claims?

options.label: Collapse equal definitions, reject unequal ones, keep equal claims
options.consequence: a graph is a map from id to definition, as Spec §3.9 makes the bus; two publishers with one source and one write set stay two claimants, so the single-writer check sees both; the catalog must report duplicate ids before building a graph

options.label: Keep every definition and report duplicates as a finding
options.consequence: the catalog gets a diagnostic for free, but every analysis keyed by topology id becomes ambiguous and the check is not in root D1's v1 list

options.label: Collapse equal claims too
options.consequence: set semantics throughout, but two identical publisher constructions, a real runtime first-claim failure, would pass the static single-writer check

chosen: Collapse equal definitions, reject unequal ones, keep equal claims
why: Spec §3.9: activating one id twice with the same declaration is the same topology, with a different one an error, so the graph mirrors the bus. Spec §3.11's runtime first-claim rejects a second publisher even when it is identical to the first, so the static view must count it. Signal that would have changed it: catalogs that legitimately hold one id in two coordination domains.

question: What shape do the analyses take: what they consume, what they return, and which checks are here?

options.label: One function per analysis over TopologyGraph, typed findings in a sealed family, plus analyzeTopologyGraph
options.consequence: cycles, self-references, writer conflicts and scope violations as final classes under sealed TopologyFinding, a fixed result order, topic name collisions over caller-supplied TopicDeclaration values; the runtime and the workspace scan call the same functions

options.label: Methods on TopologyGraph returning strings
options.consequence: compact, but untyped diagnostics that bus-api@v1 and nidana-checks@v1 would each parse

options.label: Leave single-writer to the runtime and the scan
options.consequence: matches nidana.model's Owns list literally, but ADR-002 item 8 has the scan run single-writer by calling the contracts package's analyses, the functions activation also calls

chosen: One function per analysis over TopologyGraph, typed findings in a sealed family, plus analyzeTopologyGraph
why: Root D4 and ADR-002 item 8 require activation and CI to run the same pure functions; typed sealed findings let both hosts map them to diagnostics exhaustively. Single-writer is included because ADR-002 item 8 lists it among the analyses the scan calls; nidana.model's Owns list should name it (note for the orchestrator). The guarantee that a finding-free graph stays finding-free when topologies or claims are removed (G17) lets the bus keep its active set clean by rejecting any activation or publisher whose graph has a finding.

question: What exactly is an unmediated self-read, and what does a SelfReference finding report?

options.label: Paths of non-state-bearing edges from a read to a write of the topic, every edge on them reported
options.consequence: well defined whatever the algorithm (forward reach from the read intersected with backward reach from the write); a withLatestFrom over the topology's own state is unmediated, as topology-dsl@v1's column marks it

options.label: Report one representative path
options.consequence: a shorter diagnostic, but which path is algorithm-dependent and untestable as a value

options.label: Treat a latest input of withLatestFrom as mediating
options.consequence: accepts the reducer-by-withLatestFrom pattern, which cannot loop in zero time, but contradicts topology-dsl@v1's Self-reference column and the reduceInto idiom Spec §6.3 provides

chosen: Paths of non-state-bearing edges from a read to a write of the topic, every edge on them reported
why: Spec §3.8 asks that any read of a self-written topic reach the write only through a state-bearing operator; the set of edges on unmediated paths is unique, so the finding is a value the fixtures can pin. topology-dsl@v1 fixed which stages mediate, and reduceInto is the DSL's reducer. Signal that would have changed it: real topologies that need withLatestFrom over their own state.

question: What counts as a topic name collision (Spec §4.3)?

options.label: Any two distinct declarations of one name
options.consequence: two registries declaring cart.items fail CI even with one type; the input carries a caller-chosen site so equal declarations from two places stay distinct

options.label: Only declarations whose variant or type differ
options.consequence: mirrors the runtime check, but two teams silently sharing a channel by accident would pass

chosen: Any two distinct declarations of one name
why: Spec §4.3 says the CI step fails the build on any name collision and names the runtime type check as defense in depth only.

question: Are the JSON form of a single definition and the aggregated topology-graph.json one schema or two?

options.label: One schema, one document type
options.consequence: the graph document is the only top-level form; a single definition's JSON is the object a graph document lists ($defs/topologyDefinition); one decoder entry point and one format string

options.label: Two schemas, the graph one referencing the definition one
options.consequence: a standalone definition document exists, at the cost of cross-file $ref resolution in two validators and two formats to version

options.label: One schema whose root is either form
options.consequence: both documents validate at the root, but every consumer must branch on which it got

chosen: One schema, one document type
why: Spec §6.5 renders the JSON form from the graph (graph.render(JsonRenderer())), and nothing in v1 emits a lone definition document; a graph of one definition (toGraph()) covers that use. One document keeps the CI consumers' contract to one format.

question: Who emits the aggregated topology-graph.json, and through which contract?

options.label: nidana.tooling through topic-codegen@v1
options.consequence: the file contract names the path and generator command; the content is JsonRenderer of the catalog's graph, byte for byte, so the file replay compares it like any generated file; nidana-checks@v1's scan builds or reads the same graph

options.label: nidana.tooling through nidana-checks@v1
options.consequence: the scan writes the manifest as a side output of a cli contract, whose recorded invocations compare stdout and exit codes, not generated trees

chosen: nidana.tooling through topic-codegen@v1
why: Guide C.3 lists topology-graph.json among the codegen's emitted artifacts, and ADR-002 item 8 has the workspace scan share the topology catalog with graph emission, so both read one graph. Signal that would have changed it: an app that runs the checks without running the codegen.

question: Is the JSON form closed or open to unknown keys, and how strict is the decoder about order?

options.label: Closed schema with a format string, canonical encoder, order-lenient decoder
options.consequence: every object has additionalProperties false, format is topology-ir@v1, so a v1 decoder never misreads another version; any added key is a v2; the encoder sorts set-like lists, the decoder accepts any order

options.label: Open schema, consumers ignore unknown keys
options.consequence: additive evolution within v1, but invalid/ cases lose their bite, typos pass, and a v2 document may be silently half-read

options.label: Closed and order-strict
options.consequence: one document per graph enforced at decode, but hand-edited or reordered documents fail for no semantic reason

chosen: Closed schema with a format string, canonical encoder, order-lenient decoder
why: The contract is versioned, so additions bump the version anyway; a closed schema makes the 38 invalid/ cases meaningful and the format string makes version skew loud. Canonical encoding keeps topology-graph.json byte-stable for the file contract; leniency on order costs nothing semantic. Signal that would have changed it: an external CI consumer that needs additive fields within v1.

question: How precisely does the contract fix the Mermaid and Graphviz renderings?

options.label: Exact rules pinned by goldens
options.consequence: node ids, labels, shapes, arrow order and escaping are stated and every sample's text is a golden, so consumers that embed or diff renderings (the build-time HTML graph, docs) build against fixed text; any rendering change is a v2

options.label: Structural guarantees only
options.consequence: layout freedom for the producer, but consumers' own goldens would depend on text no contract fixes

chosen: Exact rules pinned by goldens
why: Determinism is what makes generated documentation and the build-time graph reviewable, and HSDD wants the fixtures to be the mocks. Every edge, a write included, is a node inside its topology's subgraph, so every arrow to a topic names the topology that writes it. All seven Mermaid goldens parse with Mermaid 11.12.0 and all seven DOT goldens lay out with Graphviz 14.0.1, and undoing the escapes makes both fail. Signal that would have changed it: a renderer consumer that wants layout freedom more than stable text.

question: What is the signature of expectMatchesSchema, which ADR-001 item 4 names but does not type, and how do conformance cases find the schema and the valid/, invalid/ and render/ files?

options.label: expectMatchesSchema(Object? instance, String schemaPath), paths relative to the workspace root found by walking up
options.consequence: explicit, greppable paths; a binding works from the root and from a member's directory (a consumer stand-in, ADR-001 item 11); nidana.model's first phase implements it on package:json_schema

options.label: expectMatchesSchema(instance, slug: ...)
options.consequence: layout-independent call sites, but a fixture cannot validate against a schema at another path, and the slug-to-path rule is hidden in the tool

options.label: The harness supplies files and schemas
options.consequence: no I/O in the conformance library, but every binding repeats file plumbing and could supply a subset

chosen: expectMatchesSchema(Object? instance, String schemaPath), paths relative to the workspace root found by walking up
why: ADR-001 item 9 runs bindings from the workspace root, and item 11 lets consumers bind suites from their own package; walking up to the directory that holds hsdd/contract/ serves both, as T10 of the experiment shows. The signature is the one fixture.dart addition this contract needs from the replay tool.

question: How are the serialized-form fixtures laid out: where do valid/ documents come from, what do invalid/ documents mutate, and where do rendering goldens live?

options.label: Recorded samples as goldens, one small base for invalid/, render/ data files
options.consequence: each valid/ file is the producer's JsonRenderer output for a sample graph the conformance library records with the DSL, so G19 checks real output byte for byte; each invalid/ file breaks one rule of valid/forms.json; render/ holds .mmd and .dot files the behavior set reads, outside ADR-001's named sets

options.label: Hand-written valid/ documents, goldens as Dart strings
options.consequence: no data directory beyond ADR-001's sets, but the producer's output is never compared with a file, and renderings are unreadable in review

chosen: Recorded samples as goldens, one small base for invalid/, render/ data files
why: ADR-001 item 4 asks the conformance library to check the producer's real output; recording the samples and comparing exact files does that and pins the projection, the naming and the encoding at once. A 2.8 kB base keeps each invalid/ case reviewable, and each was checked to fail at the intended path under two validators. The binding is named nidana_dart_contracts_test.dart after the implementing package, as topic-model@v1's is; case names follow S06 and S07's convention. The goldens were written by the stand-in and then read; a stand-in defect would have entered them, which T14 cannot catch, so the review was by reading each file.

question: OQ-R1: do the bus's subjects keep RxDart's microtask-delayed first delivery for state and replay topics, or wrap subjects so a new subscriber receives the current value synchronously?

options.label: keep the microtask-delayed first delivery
options.consequence: RxDart sync subjects give it natively (root D9); a listener's callback never runs before listen returns, as Dart stream code assumes; the synchronous first value is getCurrentValue or getBufferedValues; consumers must not render the replayed value twice

options.label: deliver the current value synchronously during listen
options.consequence: matches the Spec's 'replays immediately' literally, but needs subject code of nidana's own, breaks the Dart convention (late final sub = stream.listen(...) patterns fail), and buys nothing on a TestBus, which is deterministic either way (ADR-003 item 6)

chosen: keep the microtask-delayed first delivery
why: The atomicity rule of Spec §3.10 holds with RxDart's timing (the replay comes first, then the values delivered meanwhile, none missed); only 'immediately' is not synchronous. A synchronous delivery inside listen would need a custom Stream that violates what Dart stream consumers assume, and nidana.flutter already takes its first frame from getCurrentValue. Stated as G17; decides OQ-R1. The signal that would have changed it: a UI adapter that cannot read getCurrentValue before subscribing.

question: OQ-R3: where does StateTopic dedup sit, given the per-read opt-out of Spec §3.12, and does an observer see a publish that dedup suppressed?

options.label: dedup per read; observers and the current value see every publish
options.consequence: the subject sees every publish, so a Dedup.none read can see an equal one; every causation id a published envelope carries points at an envelope observers saw; telemetry also sees equal-value publishes

options.label: dedup at publish with a side channel for opted-out reads; observers see changes only
options.consequence: observers and recorders see fewer no-op publishes, but a Dedup.none read can publish an output whose cause no observer saw, breaking causation-chain walking through observed envelopes

chosen: dedup per read; observers and the current value see every publish
why: topology-dsl@v1 G19 already requires a Dedup.none read to see a publish equal to the current value, so the subject must receive every publish; the remaining choice was what observers see. Spec §3.7 has observers receive every publish event, and topic-model@v1 relies on every causation id pointing at an observed envelope. Stated as G16; decides OQ-R3. The signal that would have changed it: a telemetry cost profile where equal-value publishes dominate exported spans. Upstream: Spec §3.12 is silent on observers.
evidence: hsdd/contract/topic-model.md (How the lineage functions are applied)

question: How does the Interface make a publisher-less publish, and a publisher's publish, unable to reach a StateTopic, as Spec §2.4 requires?

options.label: amend topic-model@v1 with a sealed MultiWriterTopic<T> above EventTopic<T> and ReplayTopic<T>, and take it in publish
options.consequence: type-level: a state topic does not compile; the Spec's single publish(topic, value) shape survives; costs a compatible amendment of topic-model@v1 before bus-api@v1's fixtures compile

options.label: take Topic<T> and throw ArgumentError for a StateTopic
options.consequence: self-contained, no amendment, but the misuse surfaces at first run rather than at compile time, and the guarantee becomes a behavior case

options.label: one method per variant (publishEvent, publishReplay)
options.consequence: type-level without an amendment, but departs from the Spec's and the Guide's single publish name and doubles the surface

chosen: amend topic-model@v1 with a sealed MultiWriterTopic<T> above EventTopic<T> and ReplayTopic<T>, and take it in publish
why: Spec §2.4 says there is no publisher-less path to a StateTopic and that a publisher reaches one only through a writer handle; the owner's practice favors type-level proof (Rationale §3.3), and the step brief names this as a type-level reject fixture. Dart has no union types and topic-model@v1's Topic family is sealed, so only topic-model can declare the supertype. The amendment is compatible: switches over Topic stay exhaustive. Reject codes confirmed against a stand-in carrying it. If the amendment is declined, the fallback is the ArgumentError option, with no_publisherless_state_publish.dart and the first line of publisher_reaches_state_through_writer.dart turned into behavior cases.

question: Where is the boundary between bus-api@v1 and bus-testing@v1, given ADR-003's closed set of two providers and a TestBus that is a bus?

options.label: main library to bus-api, testing.dart to bus-testing, with SchedulerProvider sealed across both and Bus final with TestBus as its one subtype, declared in one src library
options.consequence: the closed provider set and 'TestBus is a Bus' hold by the language; bus-testing must declare its two types in the same implementation library as bus-api's

options.label: an open SchedulerProvider interface and an implementable Bus
options.consequence: simpler library layout, but applications could define providers that break the quiescence and cancellation rules (ADR-003 alternatives) and fake buses that bypass ordering and ownership

chosen: main library to bus-api, testing.dart to bus-testing, with SchedulerProvider sealed across both and Bus final with TestBus as its one subtype, declared in one src library
why: ADR-003 item 1 fixes exactly two providers; ADR-002 item 3 puts TestBus and the virtual scheduler in testing.dart. Dart's sealed and final are checked against the declaring library, so one src library with split exports gives both. BusConfig.scheduler is nullable so TestBus(config) can tell an unset provider from an explicit production one, which ADR-003 item 6 has it reject.

question: Is Bus an implementable interface (stand-ins, mocks) or a final class?

options.label: final class, TestBus its only subtype
options.consequence: no hand-written fake can bypass delivery, ordering or ownership; consumers test on a TestBus, as the Spec intends

options.label: abstract interface with a factory constructor
options.consequence: consumers could mock the bus with a mocking library before the runtime exists, at the cost of fakes that drift from the guarantees

chosen: final class, TestBus its only subtype
why: HSDD's rule is that the fixtures are the mocks, and Spec §3.6 and Appendix A.7 make TestBus the test substrate; every consumer in the tree has a hard edge on the real runtime or waits for its first phase (root D10). The signal that would have changed it: a consumer that must test against the bus before nidana.runtime's first phase merges.

question: How are dev-mode diagnostics typed so that other nidana packages can report through the bus's sink (root D8)?

options.label: sealed BusDiagnostic with final runtime variants plus a base ShellDiagnostic other packages extend, delivered through reportDiagnostic
options.consequence: the runtime's variants stay exhaustively switchable; navigation and Flutter add their own subclasses without touching bus-api

options.label: a closed sealed family only
options.consequence: exhaustive, but other packages could not report through the sink D8 says they read

options.label: an open interface
options.consequence: anyone can add variants, so no consumer can switch exhaustively

chosen: sealed BusDiagnostic with final runtime variants plus a base ShellDiagnostic other packages extend, delivered through reportDiagnostic
why: Root D8 says every nidana package with dev-mode behavior reads dev mode and the sink from the bus it holds, and that diagnostics are values of a sealed type. A sealed base with one base-class extension point gives both; reportDiagnostic does nothing outside dev mode so callers need not check. Diagnostics carry no payload, so nothing needs redaction (Spec §9.2 item 2).

question: What do the throws the Specification requires look like on Dart?

options.label: a sealed BusError family (ActivationRejected, ClaimRejected, TopologyConflict, TopicCollision, BusLimitExceeded) carrying findings, plus SDK ArgumentError and StateError for misuse
options.consequence: callers and tests match on typed causes with topology-ir@v1's findings attached; removeTopic returns false rather than throwing when refused

options.label: SDK errors only (StateError, ArgumentError)
options.consequence: smaller surface, but a caller cannot tell a cycle from a writer conflict without parsing messages

chosen: a sealed BusError family (ActivationRejected, ClaimRejected, TopologyConflict, TopicCollision, BusLimitExceeded) carrying findings, plus SDK ArgumentError and StateError for misuse
why: Spec §3.11 has the rejection name the current owner, which the WriterConflict finding carries; root D8 keeps these as throws. They extend Error because each is a configuration bug the CI checks should have caught. Spec §7.5 lets removal return false per platform convention, which reads naturally in Dart.

question: How is reentrant publish normalization realized: which publishes are reentrant, and how are deferred publishes ordered?

options.label: a publish made during a delivery joins one per-bus FIFO drained by one provider-zone microtask, including the publishes the drain itself causes; timer-driven publishes are not reentrant
options.consequence: fan-out emissions stay consecutive with no intervening publish (Spec §3.3); a delivery of a publish is the unit of reentrancy

options.label: one scheduleMicrotask per reentrant publish, as Spec §3.4's table reads
options.consequence: simplest, but a microtask some subscriber schedules can run between two emissions of one fan-out

options.label: defer every publish while the queue is non-empty
options.consequence: call order equals delivery order even across shell publishes, but a shell publish becomes asynchronous whenever anything is pending

chosen: a publish made during a delivery joins one per-bus FIFO drained by one provider-zone microtask, including the publishes the drain itself causes; timer-driven publishes are not reentrant
why: Spec §3.3 promises fan-out in declaration order with no intervening external publishes, and Spec §3.4 normalizes reentrant publishes to the next scheduling boundary. One FIFO drained in one microtask satisfies both, avoids RxDart's same-subject StateError and depth-first delivery (root D9), and makes publishes made in sequence consecutive (G14), which the navigation executor's paired writes rely on (Guide §3.4).

question: What does the startup barrier hold back: only shell publishers' publishes, as Spec §3.13 words it, or every publish?

options.label: every publish, a topology's and a publisher-less one included; the connection and observed first values are not publishes and are not held
options.consequence: nothing reaches a subscriber or an observer before start, so activation order before start is irrelevant for every variant (Rationale §3.1)

options.label: shell publishers' publishes only
options.consequence: the literal wording, but a topology's output from its connection would be delivered before start and an APPLICATION reader activated later could miss it

chosen: every publish, a topology's and a publisher-less one included; the connection and observed first values are not publishes and are not held
why: Spec §3.13 says nothing is delivered before start and that activation order is irrelevant for APPLICATION topologies; the only topology publishes before start come from activation connections, and holding them back is what makes the order irrelevant (G34 runs both orders and compares). Upstream: Spec §3.13 should say every publish is queued.

question: Spec §3.9: when is a second activation under the same topologyId 'the same declaration', given that definitions do not see a scan seed, closure bodies or two functions with one name?

options.label: equal topology-ir@v1 definitions are the same declaration; declare runs once more for the check
options.consequence: the DI double-registration case returns the same handle; differences the IR cannot see are not detected

options.label: the same Topology object (identity)
options.consequence: detects nothing new, and turns two instances of one topology class, the motivating case, into an error

options.label: equal definitions and the same runtime type
options.consequence: catches two classes with one id and equal wiring, but the builder form has one runtime type for every topology

chosen: equal topology-ir@v1 definitions are the same declaration; declare runs once more for the check
why: The bus can compare only what the IR records; Dart cannot compare closures. Spec §3.9's motivation is one topology registered twice, usually as two instances. Stated as G23 with the limitation spelled out and a case that shows two scan seeds sharing a handle. The signal that would have changed it: a reported bug where two different closures under one id silently shared a handle. Upstream: Spec §3.9 should say observable differences are judged on the IR.

question: Spec §4.3's runtime name check throws on 'a different type'. Does a second declaration of the same name and type that differs in its sensitive flag, tracing, dedup or buffer size collide?

options.label: collide on variant, value type, sensitive, tracing, dedup or buffer size
options.consequence: a second declaration that drops the sensitive flag cannot share a subject and leak envelopes to non-sensitive observers

options.label: collide on variant and value type only
options.consequence: the literal rule; equal topics (topic-model@v1 G7) with different flags would share one subject, and the flag on each envelope would depend on which declaration published it

chosen: collide on variant, value type, sensitive, tracing, dedup or buffer size
why: envelope.sensitive comes from the topic object used at the publish (MessageEnvelope.publishedTo), so two declarations differing in the flag would mix sensitive and non-sensitive envelopes on one subject, which Spec §9.2's gating cannot recover from. Upstream: Spec §4.3 should name the declaration fields.

question: How do maxTopics (Spec §11.3, 'activate fails if exceeded') and getCurrentValue's 'never throws' (Spec §2.5) combine?

options.label: activation over the limit throws BusLimitExceeded; any other access over it creates the subject and reports TopicLimitExceeded in dev mode
options.consequence: getCurrentValue keeps its never-throws rule; a topic-creating loop still shows up, in dev mode and at the next activation

options.label: every subject creation over the limit throws
options.consequence: a hard cap everywhere, contradicting Spec §2.5 for getCurrentValue

chosen: activation over the limit throws BusLimitExceeded; any other access over it creates the subject and reports TopicLimitExceeded in dev mode
why: Spec §11.3 names activation only, and Spec §2.5 forbids getCurrentValue from throwing; the diagnostic keeps the guardrail visible. getCurrentValue still throws TopicCollision, which Spec §4.3 requires. The limit defaults are the Spec §11.3 example values. Upstream: the Spec should say how the cap and getCurrentValue interact.

question: Does a shell publish carry causation, as Spec §2.4's PaymentResult example suggests, or is it always a root message?

options.label: always a root message: fresh correlation, no causation
options.consequence: matches Guide §3.6 (a page's publish is a root publish); shell code never needs envelopes; a service's result is not linked to the intent that prompted it

options.label: link it to the delivery in progress through an ambient context
options.consequence: reconstructs the Spec's example chain for synchronous handlers, but async work loses the context and every delivery would need a zone or a stack

options.label: an explicit causedBy argument on publish
options.consequence: precise, but shell code would need envelopes, which observed streams do not carry

chosen: always a root message: fresh correlation, no causation
why: Guide §3.6 states that the bus does not link a page's publish to the intent that opened it, and Guide §10.2 lists that link as an open observability convenience. Observed streams carry payloads only (Refinement 4). Listed under Versioning as a candidate for a later version.

question: What does Tracing.disabled do on this bus?

options.label: its envelopes reach no observer and a pipeline reading it starts a new flow; the envelopes still carry generated metadata
options.consequence: the observable rule of Guide §8.1 holds; the TestBus recorder can still show untraced values with ids, which topology-dsl@v1's live G25 case needs

options.label: placeholder metadata (empty ids, no timestamp)
options.consequence: saves id generation and a clock read, but no allocation, because a Dart envelope holds its payload

chosen: its envelopes reach no observer and a pipeline reading it starts a new flow; the envelopes still carry generated metadata
why: Spec §3.5 Cost describes a singleton untracked envelope; in Dart the envelope holds the payload, so no allocation is saved. topic-model@v1 fixes the lineage rule and S06 noted observers must not see untraced envelopes; the live suite watches an untraced topic and compares its correlation id.

question: What shape does the module scope API that UI adapters bind route events to take (Spec §7.3)?

options.label: bus.module(id, topologies, gracePeriod) returning one ModuleScope per id; acquire() returns a ModuleReference token whose release counts once
options.consequence: double releases from route lifecycles cannot drive the count negative; a failed activation leaves the count at zero

options.label: acquire() and release() counters on the scope
options.consequence: smaller surface, but a duplicated release silently tears the module down

options.label: an id-less scope object held by the adapter
options.consequence: no registry, but two widgets of one module subtree would keep separate counts

chosen: bus.module(id, topologies, gracePeriod) returning one ModuleScope per id; acquire() returns a ModuleReference token whose release counts once
why: Spec §7.3 makes reference counting the only correct pattern and warns about double mount and unmount in React StrictMode; tokens make release idempotent per reference. Modules take module-scoped topologies only (Spec §7.2). The signal that would have changed it: flutter-binding@v1 needing to release without holding the reference.

question: Spec §2.4: 'a publisher bound to a module or page scope releases it with that scope'. Does bus-api@v1 bind publishers to module scopes?

options.label: no: scope is declared on the publisher for the analyses, and the caller disposes it when it releases the module or the page unmounts
options.consequence: no lifecycle surface without a consumer; a page adapter disposes its publishers itself

options.label: ModuleScope.publisher(...) disposed at module teardown
options.consequence: automatic release, but the shell component would hold a publisher that dies after the grace period and must obtain a new one on re-entry

chosen: no: scope is declared on the publisher for the analyses, and the caller disposes it when it releases the module or the page unmounts
why: Every shell-owned state topic Spec §3.11 lists (executor, connectivity, location, permissions, migration bridge) is application-level; nidana.flutter owns page publishers and disposes them on unmount. Listed under Versioning as a candidate. The signal that would have changed it: a module or page that claims a state topic.

question: Is the SDK-neutral telemetry observer (root D1) part of bus-api@v1, and how does it see activations when BusObserver has only onPublish?

options.label: TelemetryObserver in the main library, plus an ActivationObserver interface the bus also notifies
options.consequence: the full Guide §8.2 mapping, activation spans included, without touching topic-model@v1's BusObserver

options.label: TelemetryObserver with publish spans only
options.consequence: no new interface, but the Guide's activation row is dropped

options.label: add onActivate to BusObserver
options.consequence: one interface, but a breaking change to topic-model@v1, which applications implement

chosen: TelemetryObserver in the main library, plus an ActivationObserver interface the bus also notifies
why: Root D1 puts the observer in nidana.runtime's main package and its public surface needs a contract; Guide §8.2 maps both publishes and activations onto spans. Attribute keys follow the Guide's nidana.sensitive in snake case under one nidana. prefix; spans are opened and ended within the call, since an observer has no clock.
evidence: hsdd/contract/topic-model.md (Versioning: adding a member to BusObserver is breaking)

question: Spec §7.2 says the bus enforces that APPLICATION topologies activate before start(). Does a later APPLICATION activation throw?

options.label: report LateApplicationActivation in dev mode and activate
options.consequence: the symptom shows in debug and test runs; a test that activates after start is not failed on a scope it does not exercise

options.label: throw StateError
options.consequence: strict enforcement, at the cost of every after-start activation of an APPLICATION topology, in apps and tests alike

options.label: nothing
options.consequence: silent; the activation-order hazard of Spec §3.13 goes unnoticed

chosen: report LateApplicationActivation in dev mode and activate
why: No evidence settles it. The diagnostic surfaces the hazard Spec §3.13 exists to prevent while keeping the operation total. The signal that would have changed it: the owner preferring hard enforcement, which is a compatible tightening only before v1 is stable.

question: What happens to a publish that is queued (before start, or reentrant) when its publisher is disposed or its topology deactivated?

options.label: discard it
options.consequence: a released owner's state publish can never land after a new claimant's (Spec §3.11); a service that publishes and disposes before start loses that publish

options.label: deliver it
options.consequence: every publish call is honored, but a queued state publish could be delivered after another claimant took the topic

chosen: discard it
why: Single-writer ownership is structural (Spec §3.11, Rationale §2.1); delivery after release would allow a second writer's value to interleave with the old owner's. topology-dsl@v1 G29 says a deactivated topology publishes nothing afterwards; discarding makes that hold for what subscribers observe.

question: ADR-003 left open whether shutdown() drains the virtual queue first. What does shutdown do with pending work?

options.label: deliver the bus's own pending reentrant publishes synchronously, discard the startup queue, run nothing else of the provider zone
options.consequence: works the same on both providers, needs no scheduler operation, and honors 'drains pending dispatches'

options.label: discard every pending publish
options.consequence: simplest, but drops publishes already made

options.label: run the virtual scheduler's triggerActions first on a TestBus
options.consequence: drains more on a TestBus, but behaves differently from the production provider and makes bus-api depend on bus-testing

chosen: deliver the bus's own pending reentrant publishes synchronously, discard the startup queue, run nothing else of the provider zone
why: Spec §11.2 says shutdown drains pending dispatches; ADR-003 requires shutdown not to chain on futures, and the bus's FIFO of reentrant publishes is its own, so it can be drained synchronously. Publishes queued before start were never dispatched. What a TestBus does beyond that is bus-testing@v1's.

question: ADR-003 left open whether a TestBus generates deterministic envelope ids. What does bus-api@v1 say?

options.label: ids and correlation ids are opaque and pairwise distinct; whether a TestBus makes them deterministic is bus-testing@v1's
options.consequence: bus-api's suite compares ids only by reference to observed envelopes; bus-testing@v1 decides golden-friendly ids

options.label: fix an id format here
options.consequence: deterministic ids for every bus, at the cost of fixing a production format no consumer needs

chosen: ids and correlation ids are opaque and pairwise distinct; whether a TestBus makes them deterministic is bus-testing@v1's
why: No bus-api guarantee depends on an id's value, and the TestBus is bus-testing@v1's declaration; a deterministic scheme can be an internal hook of the package.

question: How does the bus-api conformance harness let a case drive time without naming bus-testing@v1 types?

options.label: BusApiHarness with bus(config), flush, advance, pendingTimers and settle, all in bus-api and SDK types; production-provider capture tested by constructing a Bus inside a TestBus delivery
options.consequence: the library compiles against bus-api alone; the binding maps the calls to TestBus and its scheduler

options.label: let the library import testing.dart
options.consequence: fewer indirections, but the suite would not compile until bus-testing@v1 lands and could not bind any other virtual implementation

chosen: BusApiHarness with bus(config), flush, advance, pendingTimers and settle, all in bus-api and SDK types; production-provider capture tested by constructing a Bus inside a TestBus delivery
why: The step brief requires it, and ADR-001 item 4 has a harness supply factories and settle. A delivery runs in the provider zone, so a Bus constructed there captures the virtual zone and clock, which tests ADR-003 item 1 without package:clock in a fixture.

question: How does the binding of topology-dsl@v1's live suite implement LiveRun.watch, which must return envelopes, including those of a Tracing.disabled topic?

options.label: a view of the TestBus's envelope recorder from the watch on, filtered to the topic and read with its own dedup
options.consequence: works for every topic; forward-references bus-testing@v1's recorder and requires it to record untraced topics

options.label: a BusObserver per watch
options.consequence: uses bus-api only, but observers never see an untraced topic (G30), so the live G25 untraced case fails

options.label: make publish return its envelope
options.consequence: adds surface to bus-api for one binding, and still misses envelopes topologies publish

chosen: a view of the TestBus's envelope recorder from the watch on, filtered to the topic and read with its own dedup
why: The live suite's untraced case watches a Tracing.disabled topic and reads its envelope's correlation id; observers cannot see it by design, and Spec §3.5 lists the TestBus recorder as an envelope-visible party. The experiment's seeded defect (a recorder that drops untraced topics) fails that case, which makes the requirement on bus-testing@v1 explicit.

question: Forced removal and shutdown must end observed subscriptions with done; a closed RxDart BehaviorSubject delivers done from a microtask the virtual scheduler does not run. What does the contract guarantee?

options.label: the bus ends every observed subscription itself, with done delivered before removeTopic or shutdown returns
options.consequence: deterministic on every provider; the runtime wraps each observed subscription

options.label: done follows the subject's close, whenever the engine delivers it
options.consequence: no wrapper, but on a TestBus done needs a real event-loop turn, which ADR-003 item 6 rules out for anything a bus operation schedules

chosen: the bus ends every observed subscription itself, with done delivered before removeTopic or shutdown returns
why: output-close.txt shows a sync BehaviorSubject delivering done from a microtask while PublishSubject, ReplaySubject and sync controllers deliver it synchronously; the stand-in's G9 case failed after a flush until the bus closed its own per-subscription controllers. Stated in G9, G18 and G36.

question: Which assignments does the immutability reject fixture pin, given that assigning a getter reports assignment_to_final for a final field and assignment_to_final_no_setter for a getter without one?

options.label: BusConfig's fields only, which its const constructor makes final
options.consequence: the reject code does not depend on how the producer implements Bus's getters

options.label: Bus's and Publisher's getters too
options.consequence: wider coverage, but the expected code would depend on the producer's choice of fields or getters, a fixture gap the first replay would surface

chosen: BusConfig's fields only, which its const constructor makes final
why: The probe against the stand-in showed bus.clock = ... reporting nothing for a late final field and assignment_to_final for a final one; topology-ir@v1 recorded the same ambiguity. A const constructor requires final fields, so BusConfig's code is stable.

question: Dev-mode recursion detection (Spec §3.4): what happens past maxReentrancyDepth?

options.label: report ReentrancyDepthExceeded once per chain, at the hop that crosses the threshold, and keep delivering
options.consequence: dev and release builds deliver the same values; a runaway loop shows as a diagnostic and, on a TestBus, as the scheduler's action bound

options.label: stop delivering the chain in dev mode
options.consequence: a loop cannot starve the event loop in debug builds, but dev mode would change what the app does

chosen: report ReentrancyDepthExceeded once per chain, at the hop that crosses the threshold, and keep delivering
why: Spec §3.4 asks for detection and a diagnostic with the chain, not for interruption; ADR-003 item 5's action bound already surfaces a runaway loop on a TestBus.

question: Where do observers' log, metric and span calls go?

options.label: one ObserveContext per bus in BusConfig, defaulting to a context whose log prints and whose metric and span discard
options.consequence: an app plugs its telemetry backend in once; a logging observer prints out of the box

options.label: a context per observer at addObserver
options.consequence: different sinks per observer, which no v1 consumer needs

options.label: a default that discards everything
options.consequence: silent by default; a logging observer added without a context shows nothing

chosen: one ObserveContext per bus in BusConfig, defaulting to a context whose log prints and whose metric and span discard
why: Spec §3.7 gives observers out-of-band sinks without saying who supplies them; the OpenTelemetry binding is deferred (root D1), so the app supplies the sinks. No evidence beyond judgement; the signal that would have changed it: two observers needing different backends.

question: Does the runtime's main library re-export nidana_dart_contracts?

options.label: no; shell code imports both
options.consequence: each import names its package and version; consistent with topology_ir.dart not re-exporting the main contracts library

options.label: yes
options.consequence: one import for apps, at the cost of the runtime's namespace carrying every contracts declaration

chosen: no; shell code imports both
why: Judgement and consistency with topology-ir@v1's library rule; nothing in the Spec or ADR-002 asks for re-export. Compatible to add later.

question: bus-api@v1 needs topic-model@v1 to gain `sealed class MultiWriterTopic<T> extends Topic<T>` with EventTopic and ReplayTopic extending it, so that a publisher-less publish and a publisher's publish to a StateTopic do not compile (bus-api G11, G19). Is this a breaking amendment that stops the run, and do we amend or take bus-api's fallback (take Topic<T> and throw ArgumentError on a StateTopic)?

options.label: Amend topic-model@v1 now, compatibly
options.consequence: One hsdd-contract amendment step before bus-testing@v1; Spec §2.4's 'no publisher-less path to a StateTopic' becomes a compile error, consistent with the tree's typed-over-stringly reading; bus-api@v1's fixtures compile once the amendment lands.

options.label: Take bus-api's fallback
options.consequence: No amendment; the two reject fixtures become behavior cases and the rule moves from compile time to a runtime ArgumentError.

options.label: Treat it as a breaking amendment and stop
options.consequence: The run ends for the owner to decide, although no consumer code exists and the change keeps every existing exhaustive switch compiling.

chosen: Amend topic-model@v1 now, compatibly
why: The breaking-amend stop covers an amendment that would break an existing consumer. Here no consumer exists: every contract is draft, no package has been written, and the only consumers named are nodes not yet planned. The change itself is additive: MultiWriterTopic is sealed with exactly EventTopic and ReplayTopic, so a switch over Topic that names the three leaf variants stays exhaustive, and topic-model@v1's Versioning rule ('adding a variant to Topic' is breaking) does not apply because no leaf variant is added. Compile-time rejection follows Spec §1 (typed over stringly-typed) and Spec §2.4. The amendment is sequenced before bus-testing@v1 so every later contract reads the amended model.

question: bus-api@v1's two bindings call bus-testing@v1 names that do not exist yet (TestBus, TestBus.scheduler, recorder.envelopes). S09 suggests letting the bus-testing@v1 step edit bus-api's binding files if it picks other names. Allow that?
